title: Striatofugal balance and beneficial effects of facilitating nucleus accumbens mGlu4 receptor activity in the Fmr1-/- mouse model of Fragile X Syndrome.
abstract: Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is the leading monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). To date, no approved pharmacological treatment alleviates social impairments in patients with FXS. Since D1 and D2 dopamine receptor-expressing striatal projection neurons (SPNs) were shown to regulate ASD-sensitive behaviors, we explored whether the balance of activity between D1- and D2-SPNs would be biased in the Fmr1-/- mouse model of FXS. We evaluated striatal function in Fmr1-/- and Fmr1+/+ mice under pharmacological challenge and performed RNAscope® in situ hybridization following social interaction to assess the activity of SPNs in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and dorsal striatum (DS). We evidenced a decrease in D1-SPN activity, biasing the D1/D2-SPN balance. We then evaluated the effects of compounds developed to repress D2-SPN activity on behavioral impairments in Fmr1-/- mice. Systemically facilitating mGlu4 or blocking A2a receptor activity relieved behavioral deficits in this model. Moreover, social interaction in Fmr1-/- mice was fully rescued by photopharmacological activation of mGlu4 in the ventral pallidum, to which both NAc D1- and D2-SPNs project, and mGlu4 receptors in the NAc likely contributed to restoring social deficits after systemic mGlu4 facilitation. Together, these results are consistent with our working hypotheses of both biased striatal D1/D2-SPN balance in social deficit and contribution of mGlu4 receptors expressed by NAc SPNs in modulating social behavior. In conclusion, pharmacological compounds able to regulate SPN activity demonstrate a promising therapeutic potential to relieve ASD-like deficits in FXS. PHARMACOLOGICAL COMPOUNDS: ADX88178 (CAS 1235318-89-4); haloperidol hydrochloride (CAS 1511-16-6); istradefylline (CAS 155270-99-8); LSP4-2022 (CAS 1413405-33-0); morphine hydrochloride (CAS 6055-06-7); quinpirole hydrochloride (CAS 85798-08-9); SCH-23390 hydrochloride (CAS 125941-87-9); SKF-81297 hydrobromide (CAS 67287-39-2); sulpiride (CAS 15676-16-1); VU0155041 sodium (CAS 1259372-69-4); optogluram (CAS 1627840-48-5).

title: Neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy: High genetic yield and long-term outcomes in a multicenter southern European cohort.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine the genetic diagnostic yield, characterize the clinical and genetic landscape, and evaluate long-term epilepsy, neurodevelopmental, and survival outcomes in a strictly defined cohort of neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). METHODS: Retrospective multicenter observational study across tertiary epilepsy centers in Italy, Greece, and Spain. Sixty-two full-term neonates fulfilling ILAE 2022 criteria for DEE with seizure onset within the first 30 days of life and a minimum follow-up of 18 months were included. All patients underwent next-generation sequencing-based genetic testing. Genetic findings, clinical characteristics, and long-term outcomes were systematically analyzed. RESULTS: A molecular diagnosis was established in 82.2% of patients (51/62), identifying variants across 29 genes grouped, for descriptive purposes, into four broad categories according to principal biological role. First-line whole-exome sequencing achieved higher diagnostic yield than targeted gene panels (88.9% vs. 41.2%), although this comparison was influenced by differences in testing era and strategy. KCNQ2 variants were the most frequent genetic cause (29.4%), and several treatable metabolic disorders were identified. After a mean follow-up of 11.9 years, 64.5% of patients had drug-resistant epilepsy and mortality reached 17.7%. Seizure freedom was achieved in a subset of patients, particularly those with KCNQ2-related DEE. Nevertheless, severe-to-profound intellectual disability affected 71.7% of evaluable patients and persisted even among those who became seizure-free, suggesting that neurodevelopmental outcomes are influenced by factors beyond seizure burden, including the underlying genetic disorder and other disease-related factors. However, the marked variability observed precludes any causal inference from these data. SIGNIFICANCE: This large European cohort demonstrates a high genetic diagnostic yield in neonatal-onset DEE, supporting first-line whole-exome sequencing as the preferred first-tier genetic test. The persistence of severe neurodevelopmental impairment despite seizure control highlights the need for precision therapies targeting disease mechanisms in addition to seizure management. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: We studied 62 newborns who developed severe epilepsy caused by genetic changes, following them for up to 25 years. We found a genetic cause in over 80% of cases, and genetic testing that reads the entire genetic code was far more effective than tests that only look at specific genes. Although seizures improved in some children over time, nearly all had lasting intellectual disability regardless of seizure control. This suggests that the underlying genetic condition may contribute substantially to brain development in addition to the effects of seizures, although our study cannot determine the relative contribution of each factor.

title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons.
abstract: Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions1-4. Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches-Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)-showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7-46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10-6). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death6, whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

title: Regular exercise augments gut-brain communication and visceral feedback control of appetite.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Regular exercise is widely accepted to support long-term body weight management; however, the neurobiological adaptations that contribute to the beneficial effects of habitual physical activity beyond increases in energy expenditure per se remain unclear. Here, we investigated whether regular exercise alters gut-brain communication and visceral feedback control of feeding. METHODS: Mice were subjected to regular voluntary wheel running. Energy expenditure and feeding were assessed under basal conditions and following an overnight fast. Nutrients were delivered directly into the stomach by intragastric infusion. Brain-wide responses to intragastric nutrient delivery were assessed using positron emission tomography (PET). Single-cell sequencing and histological analyses were used to determine nutrient-responsive neuronal populations in the caudal brainstem. Genetic associations with body weight were evaluated using GWAS data. RESULTS: Intragastric nutrient delivery suppressed feeding more strongly in exercising mice. Brain-wide PET revealed enhanced responses to intragastric nutrients in various brain regions. Single-cell sequencing identified several nutrient-responsive caudal brainstem populations, including a previously unrecognized population marked by expression of fibrinogen C domain containing 1 (FIBCD1). Regular exercise selectively enhanced the nutrient-evoked activation of FIBCD1 neurons. Histological analyses demonstrate that FIBCD1 neurons are also present in the human brainstem, and GWAS data suggest a potential relevance of this neuron population to body-weight regulation. CONCLUSIONS: Regular exercise enhances behavioral and brain responses to intragastric nutrient delivery and sensitizes FIBCD1 neurons in the brainstem of mice. These findings reveal an exercise-associated adaptation of gut-brain communication that may contribute to improved matching of caloric intake to energy expenditure.

title: Downregulation of SIRT3 Activates Macrophage Proinflammatory Function and Exacerbates Olfactory Loss in a Mouse Model of Chronic Rhinosinusitis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Inflammation of the olfactory mucosa, rather than airflow obstruction, is a major barrier to olfactory recovery in chronic rhinosinusitis with olfactory dysfunction (CRSwOD). Macrophages, a predominant immune cell population in the olfactory mucosa, play a key role in regulating local inflammation and olfactory neuroregeneration. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the role of Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3) in modulating macrophage function and its impact on olfactory recovery in CRSwOD. METHODS: Single-cell RNA sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and untargeted metabolomics data were analyzed to characterize immune and neuronal alterations in CRSwOD, with a focus on macrophage activation states. In vivo experiments using SIRT3-deficient mice were performed to evaluate olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) integrity, while in vitro assays examined the metabolic and inflammatory profiles of SIRT3-deficient macrophages under inflammatory conditions. RESULTS: Transcriptomic analysis revealed that olfactory dysfunction was closely associated with the altered functional status of mucosal macrophages. During the progression of chronic rhinosinusitis in mice, loss of SIRT3 exacerbated OSN loss and impaired the protective role of macrophages in maintaining neuronal homeostasis. Mechanistically, SIRT3 deficiency enhanced macrophage proinflammatory activity, increased hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) expression, promoted glycolysis, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential. CONCLUSION: In a mouse model of chronic rhinosinusitis, SIRT3 modulates macrophage-mediated inflammatory metabolism within the olfactory mucosa, thereby protecting against inflammation-induced olfactory damage. These findings provide mechanistic insight into inflammation-driven olfactory dysfunction and identify SIRT3 as a potential therapeutic target for CRSwOD.

title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington's disease.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene (HTT), yet how somatic repeat instability and HTT inclusions relate to selective cell loss in the human brain remains unclear. We have developed a multimodal spatial transcriptomics approach that enables the definition of transcriptional programs with subcellular resolution, somatic CAG repeat lengths, and eight other pathology markers, including HTT inclusions, in every cell of intact brain sections. Imaging 428,173 cells in the control and HD cortex revealed the selective vulnerability of layer 5-6 (L5-6) near-projecting (NP) neurons and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons, which undergo a >50% loss that is closely linked to large somatic repeat expansions (>450 ± 55 CAGs). Intranuclear inclusions were most prevalent at intermediate somatic repeat expansions (250-350 CAGs) and were associated with broader transcriptional changes than somatic repeat expansion alone. These data provide a comprehensive resource and establish a general framework for connecting repeat expansion and protein pathology across diverse cell types.

title: Expanding the Biochemical Phenotype of ReNU Syndrome: A Case Report.
abstract: Pathogenic variants in RNU4-2, encoding for a critical component of the major spliceosome, cause a newly recognized autosomal dominant disorder. Patients with RNU4-2/ReNU syndrome exhibit global developmental delay, microcephaly, dysmorphic features, seizures, hypotonia, and multi-organ involvement. Here, we detailed clinical findings and laboratory evaluation of a 3-year-old girl harboring a common RNU4-2 pathogenic variant. Her clinical presentation and disease course were similar to previously described. Furthermore, akin to other cases, an undiagnosed mitochondrial disorder was initially suspected because of hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis during metabolic stresses and abnormalities in circulating mitochondrial markers. The patient's muscle biopsy suggested mild mitochondrial abnormalities. We employed untargeted metabolomics to further characterize the patient; to our knowledge, this is the first report including metabolomic data in a ReNU syndrome patient. Clinically relevant changes were detected in several lipids, including low concentrations of several plasmalogen species. Plasmalogen deficiency, confirmed by a targeted biochemical assay, was comparable to defects of peroxisomal plasmalogen biosynthesis. Laboratory evaluation of mitochondrial and peroxisomal function in other ReNU syndrome patients is paramount for assessing the role of these organelles, if any, in the pathophysiology of this condition.

title: HDAC3 inhibition alleviates neuroinflammation and white matter injury after subarachnoid hemorrhage through modulation of BDNF/TrkB/NF-κB signaling.
abstract: White matter injury (WMI) is a major contributor to neurological deficits after subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) is an established modulator of inflammatory responses, yet its contribution to post-SAH white matter pathology remains poorly understood. We used a rat endovascular perforation model and treated animals with RGFP966, a selective HDAC3 inhibitor. Clinical data, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and transmission electron microscopy were integrated to evaluate cellular remodeling and structural integrity. Short- and long-term neurological recovery was assessed using a systematic battery of behavioral tests, while the underlying BDNF/TrkB/NF-κB signaling axis was validated through gain- and loss-of-function experiments. HDAC3 levels were elevated in both the CSF of SAH patients and rat brain tissues, inversely correlating with myelin basic protein (MBP) expression. RGFP966 treatment effectively preserved WMI, evidenced by reduced axonal injury and improved myelin shielding, and translated to superior long-term cognitive performance. ScRNA-seq analysis identified a profound shift in the microglial and oligodendrocyte-lineage landscapes after SAH. HDAC3 inhibition effectively curbed the expansion of pro-inflammatory microglial subsets while restoring homeostatic signatures and enhancing pro-myelination programs. Mechanistically, RGFP966 upregulated BDNF expression and restored TrkB phosphorylation, thereby suppressing NF-κB-mediated neuroinflammation. Notably, BDNF knockdown abolished the protective effects of HDAC3 inhibition, whereas exogenous BDNF mimicked the anti-inflammatory and myelin-protective phenotype induced by RGFP966. In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that HDAC3 is a pivotal driver of post-SAH neuroinflammation and WMI. Inhibition of HDAC3 exerts neuroprotection by recalibrating the microglial immune microenvironment and restoring the BDNF/TrkB axis.

title: Sleep-dependent DNA methylation remodeling in basolateral amygdala fear engrams.
abstract: How sleep consolidates fear memories at the molecular level within individual engram neurons is unknown. Using activity-dependent tagging and sequencing, we profiled the DNA methylome and transcriptome of engram and non-engram nuclei from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) after contextual fear conditioning with and without post-learning sleep deprivation. Fear learning induces coordinated CpG and CpH DNA methylation remodeling specifically in engram neurons, with each showing unique temporal dynamics, revealing CpH methylation as a separate component of the engram's epigenetic signature. Interestingly, sleep deprivation partially reverses learning-induced methylation changes and impairs memory recall, indicating that sleep supports engram-specific epigenetic consolidation. Integrating the engram methylome with single-cell transcriptome profiling, we construct a multi-omic molecular atlas of the BLA fear engram and identify Mid1 as a learning- and sleep-regulated methylation target. BLA-wide and engram-specific Mid1 knockdown establishes its functional requirement for fear memory consolidation, providing an approach to identify behaviorally relevant epigenetic targets.

title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain.
abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca2+) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

title: Protocol for FLOWMIST to profile autoreactivity of mouse monoclonal and serum antibodies by flow cytometry and microscopy.
abstract: Autoantibodies recognizing surface-bound or intracellular self-antigens are a hallmark of many autoimmune diseases. Here, we present a protocol for FLOWMIST to profile the autoreactivity of mouse monoclonal and serum antibodies using primary mouse splenocytes. We describe steps for antibody staining, quantitative flow cytometric screening, and confocal microscopy to classify antibody-binding patterns. Although demonstrated using mouse splenocytes, the workflow can be readily adapted to different target cells, antibody samples, species, and secondary detection reagents. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Simpson et al.1 and Newen et al.2.

title: DINOSim: Training-Free Semantic Segmentation on Microscopy Images.
abstract: We present DINOSim, a training-free method for segmenting objects in microscopy images without the need for large annotated datasets or additional model training. DINOSim builds on the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder, which captures semantic information from images. By comparing the encoder's features of image patches to those of a user-selected reference, DINOSim generates pseudo-labels that guide semantic segmentation. Subsequently, a k-nearest neighbors framework is used to refine predictions across new images. Our experiments show that DINOSim can effectively segment previously unseen objects in diverse microscopy datasets, offering performance comparable to supervised approaches while avoiding the need for costly manual labeling. We also investigate how different choices of user prompt selection and model size affect accuracy and generalization. To make the method widely accessible, we provide an open-source napari plugin (github.com/AAitorG/napari-DINOSim), enabling researchers to apply DINOSim to their own data easily. Overall, DINOSim offers a fast, flexible and practical solution for bioimage analysis, particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings.

title: Neutrophil-Derived Arg1 Impairs CD8+ T Cell Activity in Sepsis Through mTOR-Mediated Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
abstract: BACKGROUND: This research aimed to elucidate the contribution of Arginase 1 (Arg1) to pediatric sepsis progression, specifically impacting the effector functions of CD8+ T lymphocytes. METHODS: Arg1 expression was assessed in venous blood from pediatric sepsis patients (n = 21) and healthy volunteers (n = 21). Pharmacological inhibition of Arg1 was achieved using Nor-NOHA in both sepsis patients-derived neutrophils and LPS-stimulated healthy neutrophils, followed by co-culture with CD8+ T cells. Sepsis-derived neutrophils were also treated with hArg1 monoclonal antibody (mAb). CD8+ T cell viability, exhaustion markers (PD-1/TIM-3), mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP production, autophagy, and inflammatory cytokine secretion were systematically evaluated. RESULTS: Arg1 expression was markedly upregulated in sepsis patients correlated positively with neutrophil counts but negatively with CD8+ T cell numbers and mitochondrial function. Strikingly, CD8+ T cells from Arg1-high patients exhibited increased PD-1+TIM-3+ double-positive populations. Both Nor-NOHA-mediated Arg1 inhibition and hArg1-mAb neutralization significantly restored CD8+ T cell mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), ATP production, and effector cytokine secretion, while concurrently reducing PD-1/TIM-3 expression. CONCLUSION: Our findings indicate that overexpression of Arg1 derived from neutrophils leads to a highly inflammatory response suggesting that Arg1 is a potential prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in pediatric sepsis.

title: Alzheimer's disease genetics converges on microglial and neuronal dysregulation.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, with global case numbers projected to reach 153 million in 20501. AD is highly heritable, with twin-based heritability estimates of 60-80%2. Although 1,200 causal loci are predicted to exist for AD3, approximately 80 loci have been associated with AD in two recent studies4,5. Low single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based heritability estimates have prompted the suggestion that little further common-variant risk remains to be found6. Here we analysed data from 109,479 cases, 74,141 proxy cases, 2,131,799 controls and 499,708 proxy controls from diverse ancestries, identifying 118 loci in a multi-ancestry analysis and 9 additional loci in ancestry-specific analyses, 48 of which are new. We identified new AD risk genes, prioritized potential drug targets, and found that genes upregulated in microglia and downregulated in neurons in cases compared with controls were enriched for AD-associated genetic risk. Moreover, we improved polygenic prediction and estimated a SNP heritability of 16%, nearly threefold higher than previous estimates. Together, our findings show that the common-variant contribution to AD has been substantially underestimated, and reveal new molecular and cellular mechanisms as well as specific targets for future drug development research.

title: A multimodal MRI study of DTI-ALPS and cerebral blood flow changes across the Alzheimer's disease continuum.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by cerebral blood flow (CBF) abnormalities and alterations in the neurofluid-related brain tissue environment, but their evolution along the AD continuum and links to cognitive decline and plasma biomarkers remain unclear. Using multimodal MRI, we quantified the diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and CBF alterations and examined their associations with cognitive performance and plasma biomarkers across the AD continuum. METHODS: This study enrolled 78 healthy controls (HC), 53 subjective cognitive decline (SCD), 40 mild cognitive impairment (MCI), 110 AD. All subjects received MRI and neurocognitive assessments. The DTI-ALPS index was used as a diffusion-based marker of directional water diffusivity within periventricular white matter and the neurofluid-related tissue environment. CBF changes were calculated, and plasma biomarkers associated with neurodegeneration were measured. Partial correlation analysis explored relationships among ALPS index, CBF in cognition-related brain regions, cognitive scores, and plasma biomarkers. Statistical mediation analyses were performed to assess indirect effects involving the ALPS index and plasma biomarkers in the association between regional CBF and cognitive performance. RESULTS: ALPS index decreased stage-dependently along the AD continuum, significantly lower in MCI and AD versus HC and SCD. HC and SCD showed higher CBF than AD in right middle cingulate and left inferior parietal lobule. CBF in bilateral angular gyri and right superior frontal gyrus positively correlated with MoCA and RAVLT scores. Cognition-related CBF positively correlated with bilateral mean ALPS index, and negatively with NfL and p-tau217. Statistical mediation analyses identified significant indirect effects involving the bilateral mean ALPS index and plasma NfL in the association between regional CBF and cognitive performance. DISCUSSION: Cerebral hypoperfusion, altered DTI-ALPS measures, and axonal injury were closely associated across the AD continuum, suggesting interrelated neurovascular, neurofluid-related tissue, and neurodegenerative alterations associated with cognitive impairment.

title: FTO deficiency mediates ferroptosis to exacerbate cobalt-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: Cobalt, a toxic environmental contaminant, has been implicated in human neurological damage. However, the detailed molecular basis of cobalt-triggered neurotoxicity remains poorly uncovered. In the present study, we elucidated the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) demethylase fat mass and obesity-associated protein (FTO) downregulation mediates the activation of ferroptosis to drive cobalt-triggered neurodegeneration. We established an in vitro model using H4 cells and an in vivo model using C57BL/6 mice. Animal experiments provided initial evidence underscoring the critical involvement of ferroptosis in cobalt-associated neurotoxicity. Furthermore, in vitro assays revealed that ferroptosis is triggered subsequent to oxidative stress induced by cobalt exposure. Notably, MeRIP-seq profiling of H4 cells and mouse cortex revealed that ferroptosis-associated genes exhibited differential m6A modification, suggesting m6A modification might be involved in modulating ferroptosis. Concurrently, Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment analyses revealed that genes bearing differential m6A modifications were significantly clustered within pathways linked to ferroptosis as well as neurodegenerative diseases. Moreover, we found that FTO depletion effectively enhanced ferroptosis following cobalt-induced oxidative stress. Mechanistically, FTO depletion enhanced m6A modification of GPX4 and transferrin receptor protein 1 (TFRC) mRNAs, leading to reduced GPX4 and elevated TFRC expression, which aggravated cobalt-induced ferroptosis. More importantly, we observed that central nervous system specific knockout of Fto exacerbated cobalt-induced neurobehavioral deficits and neuropathological damage through ferroptosis activation. Collectively, these results provide important insights into cobalt-induced neurotoxicity by targeting FTO deficiency-mediated ferroptosis and offer an innovative strategy for investigating neurodegenerative processes driven by environmental toxicants.

title: The characteristics of perivascular proinflammation in 4-repeat tauopathies.
abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and corticobasal degeneration (CBD) are both neurodegenerative diseases characterized by aggregates composed of 4-repeat (4R) tau protein. They have distinct neuropathological features and classic clinical symptoms; however, the signs and symptoms overlap across the two syndromes. Accumulating evidence suggests that dysregulated immune response is a major contributing factor to neurodegeneration but its role in 4R-tauopathies remains undetermined. The aim is to explore the involvement of neuroinflammation from a vascular perspective in 4R-tauopathies. Autopsies from four controls, three PSP, and three CBD cases were assessed. Samples were obtained from the superior/middle frontal gyrus (S/M-FG) and basal ganglia (BG). Immunofluorescence staining included neuroinflammatory markers: glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1), cluster of differentiation 68 (CD68); vascular markers: collagen type IV (ColIV), monocarboxylate transporter-1 (MCT1), and α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA). Maximally projected confocal z-stack images of vasculature were used as a mask to quantify total perivascular GFAP+/Iba1+/CD68+ labeling. GFAP immunoreactivity ratio between MCT1 and αSMA double labeled arteries and veins was quantified to further differentiate venular and arteriolar involvement into proinflammatory activation. Both PSP and CBD had widespread perivascular proinflammatory changes, although greater in CBD. The activated GFAP+ astrocytes and microglia/macrophages in CBD were distributed extensively in S/M-FG and BG, with S/M-FG WM more affected. In PSP, abundant neuroinflammation was found in BG. The involvement of vasculature type was distinct among the two 4R-tauopathies, while CBD showed comparable proinflammatory changes in arterioles and venules, PSP exhibited predominant proinflammation in venules. The regional pattern of perivascular proinflammation differed between PSP and CBD, corresponding to the characteristic affected brain regions. CBD had more severe perivascular proinflammation that involved both arterioles and venules, while venules were more affected in PSP. Perivascular proinflammation may be a critical pathophysiological process in 4R-tauopathies.

title: Single-Cell Dissection of Microglial Dysfunction in Diabetes-Associated Neurodegenerative Vulnerability.
abstract: The molecular mechanisms linking type 2 diabetes to increased neurodegenerative risk remain poorly defined. Given the critical involvement of microglial dysfunction in neurodegeneration, we constructed a temporal single-cell atlas integrating transcriptomic and epigenomic profiles of microglia from diabetic (db/db) and control (db/m) mice across the lifespan. We delineated a nonlinear, diabetes-specific pathological trajectory characterized by early inflammatory activation, a mid-stage inflection in neurodegeneration-associated signaling and metabolic stress, and late-stage dysfunction. Chromatin accessibility profiling revealed early and persistent epigenomic priming of neurodegeneration-associated pathways, accompanied by stage-specific enhancer rewiring. Pseudotime analysis identified a disease-associated microglial (DAM) state as a candidate transition node, characterized by biased polarization and accelerated maturation under diabetic conditions. Targeted validation using freshly isolated microglia and primary microglial cultures further supported the early expansion of the DAM population, a bias toward homeostatic-to-DAM activation, and Arhgap15-dependent regulation of phagocytic activity. Together, these findings identify microglial states and candidate regulatory pathways that may link diabetes to neurodegenerative vulnerability.

title: Riluzole-Derived Benzo[d]thiazoles as CK1δ Inhibitors for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis-Related Neurodegeneration.
abstract: Riluzole-derived benzo[d]thiazoles were investigated as metabolite-inspired CK1δ inhibitors, a kinase involved in TDP-43 phosphorylation and therefore relevant to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Starting from the known CK1δ activity of riluzole, we examined whether its major hydroxylamine metabolite could preserve target recognition and provide a rational entry point for scaffold optimisation. The metabolite retained CK1δ inhibition, but its limited chemical stability and toxicity in neuronal cells identified the hydroxylamine group as a critical liability. Replacement of this functionality with a hydrazine converted the fragile metabolite-derived structure into a more potent and tractable CK1δ inhibitor series. Structure-activity relationship studies revealed that the hydrazine moiety accommodates broader substitution than the hydroxylamine counterparts, with branched alkyl and benzyl groups giving the most balanced profiles. Docking and molecular dynamics suggested that the improvement could be attributed to an additional hydrogen-bond with Gly86 in the hinge region. The best derivative combined submicromolar CK1δ inhibition with passive blood-brain barrier permeability, short-term cellular tolerance, ATP competitive inhibition, direct target engagement, and preliminary selectivity over GSK3β. Although this compound did not result neuroprotective in an oxidative stress model, it paves the way for a focused benzo[d]thiazole platform for probing CK1δ biology in ALS.

title: KCNH1 variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders exhibit prominent gain of function.
abstract: Pathogenic variants in KCNH1, encoding the human ether-á-go-go voltage-gated potassium channel (EAG1, KV10.1), are associated with the neurodevelopmental disorders Temple-Baraitser syndrome (TBS), Zimmermann-Laband syndrome (ZLS), epileptic encephalopathy, and other undefined neurodevelopmental disorders. Investigating the functional consequences of KCNH1 variants can provide information about molecular and cellular pathophysiological mechanisms and help guide therapeutic directions. In this study, we determined the functional properties of 26 disease-associated KCNH1 variants including three recurrent and six that were previously unpublished. Findings were compared to the wildtype (WT) channel along with six rare population variants. Our approach used automated patch clamp recording of heterologously expressed KCNH1 variants in both the homozygous state (variant alone) and the clinically-relevant heterozygous state (variant co-expressed with WT channels). We also examined the impact of alternative splice isoforms on functional consequences of specific variants. We demonstrated that the majority of disease-associated KCNH1 variants exhibit features consistent with gain-of-function including hyperpolarized voltage-dependence of activation, accelerated activation kinetics, or both that promote hyperpolarization of the resting membrane potential. By contrast, one unique variant discovered previously in an autism cohort had a depolarized voltage-dependence of activation and was associated with a depolarized resting potential in cells. Pharmacological testing of KCNH1 variants demonstrated differences in potency for channel block by imipramine and an investigational non-selective potassium channel blocker (LY97241) for specific variants. Collectively, our findings support gain-of-function as the most common, albeit not exclusive, molecular mechanism underlying KCNH1-related disorders and suggest opportunities for potential therapeutic drug repurposing strategies for these conditions.

title: Domain-associated phenotypic patterns with MACF1 variants.
abstract: PURPOSE: While heterozygous de novo missense variants in the microtubule-binding GAR domain of Microtubule-actin cross-linking factor 1 (MACF1) cause Lissencephaly 9 with Complex Brainstem Malformations (LIS9) [MIM 618325], the phenotypic impact of variants outside this domain remains unclear. METHODS: We assembled a cohort of 5 affected individuals from 4 unrelated families with biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants who exhibit partially overlapping yet unique phenotypic traits. A sixth individual with a de novo, heterozygous frameshift variant was additionally identified. Combined with previously reported cases, we analyzed genotype and phenotype data from 22 individuals using Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)-based unsupervised hierarchical clustering. RESULTS: Clustering revealed two distinct phenotypic signatures, suggesting domain-associated effects. Variants outside the GAR domain associate with broader neurodevelopmental phenotypes and craniofacial and skeletal involvement. Enrichment analysis (p < 0.001) using OMIM HPO sets supported these findings. In contrast to the GAR domain's strong correlation with LIS9, biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants were linked to distinct developmental anomalies. CONCLUSION: These results expand the phenotypic spectrum of MACF1-related disorders and provide preliminary evidence for domain-associated MACF1 variant effects. While limited by sample size and lack of functional validation, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and underscore the utility of HPO-based clustering for systematic phenotype comparison as additional cases emerge. Comprehensive genetic and phenotypic assessments are essential for understanding the role of MACF1 in development, informing diagnosis, and guiding future research on cytoskeletal regulation in neurodevelopment.

title: Leptin drives osteoarthritis pain through sensory neuron reprogramming independent of cartilage signaling.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Pain in osteoarthritis (OA) is often discordant with structural joint damage, particularly in obesity, where adipose-derived signals may drive nociception independently of cartilage pathology. Leptin has been demonstrated to be necessary, but not sufficient, to drive obesity-associated OA. Here, we tested the hypothesis that leptin mediates OA-associated pain through sensory neuron reprogramming rather than chondrocyte-intrinsic signaling, suggesting a fat-sensory nerve axis. DESIGN: Male and female chondrocyte-specific leptin receptor knockout mice (Aggrecan-CreERT2;LepRfl/fl) and constitutive leptin-deficient (Ob/Ob), heterozygous (Ob/+), and wild-type (WT) mice were challenged with destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) to induce OA. Pain-related behaviors, joint pathology, serum cytokines, and lumbar dorsal root ganglia (DRG) transcriptomes were assessed. Human DRG cultures treated with leptin underwent transcriptomic profiling. Leptin and leptin receptor expression was investigated in human infrapatellar fat pad and synovium single-cell datasets. RESULTS: Chondrocyte-specific deletion of the leptin receptor did not alter structural joint pathology or pain. In contrast, complete leptin deficiency (Ob/Ob) produced more severe structural damage following DMM while markedly reducing pain sensitivity. Comparing DMM limbs of Ob/+ animals to those of Ob/Ob animals, Modified Mankin score was 24.95% higher (95% CI 2.02-11.49) indicating greater structural damage, while pressure-pain thresholds were 37.5% higher (95% CI, 23.92-54.46g), indicating attenuated pain, together demonstrating dissociation between structural pathology and nociception. Circulating cytokines did not differ by genotype between Ob/+ and Ob/Ob mice, providing no systemic inflammatory signature corresponding to their divergent pain phenotypes. Mouse DRGs exhibited genotype-associated transcriptional differences, with Ob/+ DRGs enriched for lipid metabolism, eicosanoid, and inflammatory programs, whereas Ob/Ob DRGs were characterized by cytoskeletal remodeling and altered neuronal signaling. In human DRG cultures, acute leptin exposure was associated with enrichment of neuronal and nociceptor-associated transcriptional programs, whereas vehicle-treated cultures were enriched for inflammatory signaling. Human infrapatellar fat pad and synovium transcriptomic data demonstrated adipocyte-enriched leptin expression and broad leptin receptor distribution across stromal, vascular, immune, and adipocyte populations. CONCLUSIONS: In mice, leptin contributes to OA pain independently of chondrocyte-intrinsic signaling and structural disease severity. These findings identify leptin-associated neuronal programs linked to nociceptor sensitization and support further investigation of adipose-joint-sensory neuron signaling as a mediator of obesity-associated OA pain.

title: hucMSC-derived exosomes rescue cognitive impairment and Alzheimer-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice via metabolic remodeling.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. We combined behavioral tests, pathological assays and untargeted metabolomics to investigate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of hucMSC-exosomes in APP/PS1 AD mice. Seven-month-old male APP/PS1 mice were randomly divided into AD-vehicle and AD-hucMSC-exosome groups, with age-matched C57BL/6 mice as wild-type controls. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). Untargeted metabolomic analysis of brain tissues revealed that 6 primary carbon, 8 primary nitrogen and 3 secondary metabolites were common differential metabolites across the two comparison cohorts (AD-vehicle vs. WT, AD-hucMSC-exosome vs. AD-vehicle), and their aberrant expression in AD mice was all reversed by hucMSC-exosomes. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

title: A droplet-based long-read single-cell epigenome sequencing method for the high-throughput profiling of multidimensional regulatory elements within individual cells.
abstract: Recently, long-read sequencing methods have revolutionized genomic research by allowing the resolution of previously inaccessible regions across the genome. However, the throughput and scalability of these methods have hindered their general application in the field. To address this limitation, we developed droplet-based methods for the single-cell profiling of chromatin accessibility (droplet-based single-cell Nanopore ATAC-seq, dscNanoATAC) and histone modifications (droplet-based single-cell NanoCUT&Tag, dscNanoCUT) by combining a commercial microfluidic device and long-read sequencing platform, achieving a throughput of ~5000 cells in a single experiment and significantly reducing the time and costs compared with previous techniques. With cultured mammalian cells, we demonstrated the ability of dscNanoATAC and dscNanoCUT to detect allele-specific epigenetics, neighboring co-accessibility, and regulatory elements within low-mappability regions. Furthermore, leveraging the haplotype-resolved data generated from dscNanoATAC, we optimized a deep-learning model to predict allele-specific three-dimensional genome structures with high resolution (10 kb). We also applied dscNanoATAC and dscNanoCUT in complex tissues using the mouse brain as an example, and characterized the allele-specific regulation of the imprinting gene Ube3a in neurons, obtaining insights into the mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis of Prader-Willi and Angelman syndrome. With dscNanoCUT, we systematically evaluated the activity of transposon elements and revealed their potential regulatory functions in the mouse brain. Together, dscNanoATAC and dscNanoCUT serve as a versatile and scalable long-read epigenome sequencing platform, enabling multidimensional analyses of elements ranging from chromatin accessibility to histone modifications and their interplay between chromatin structures. This platform may advance our understanding of epigenetic regulation in complex biological systems.

title: CellMarker 3.0: an updated resource of manually curated and computationally predicted cell markers in human/mouse and interactive web tools for single-cell and spatial transcriptomics analysis.
abstract: The updated CellMarker 3.0 resource (http://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/CellMarker) offers a comprehensive resource, integrating experimentally validated and robustly algorithm-predicted marker genes for diverse cell types across human and mouse tissues. In addition, web tools for analyzing single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) data are described. CellMarker 3.0 was updated with more data and new features, including (i) appending 274 tissues, 1877 cell types, 64 040 markers, and 1 245 923 tissue-cell type-marker entries over the previous version. The current release contains 930 tissues, 4455 cell types, and 90 955 cell markers, resulting in a total of 1 329 284 tissue-cell type-marker entries. (ii) Expanding the resource to include computationally predicted cell-type markers derived from six algorithms, namely Spapros, Seurat::FindAllMarkers, SEMITONES, Cepo, CelliD, and COSG. (iii) New marker information was incorporated from 168 sequencing technologies, such as CEL-Seq2 and SNARE-seq. (iv) Covering 35 types of cell markers, including protein-coding genes, rRNAs, and pseudogenes. (v) The cell tool module was comprehensively restructured and upgraded, with the original six scRNA-seq analysis modules systematically optimized and two new spatial transcriptomics modules, Spatial Expression, and Spatial Chat, added. CellMarker 3.0 is a valuable resource that integrates cell identity identification, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial transcriptomics analysis.

title: M6A-modified lncRNA RMRP facilitates mitophagy and promotes ox-LDL-induced endothelial cell injury by interacting with PTBP1 and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Endothelial cell dysfunction has been identified as a major risk factor for atherosclerosis. The long non-coding RNA (LncRNA) RNA component of mitochondrial RNA processing endoribonuclease (RMRP) has been detected in mitochondria and is closely associated with inflammation and autophagy. However, the role of the lncRNA RMRP in endothelial cell injury and its potential molecular mechanisms remain unclear. METHODS: Mouse aortic endothelial cells (MAECs) were treated with oxidised low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL). Changes in cell viability, proinflammatory cytokine levels, mitophagy, and mitochondrial membrane potential in MAECs were assessed to investigate the effects of lncRNA RMRP and protein kinase B (AKT3) on endothelial injury. Knockdown and overexpression experiments were performed to determine the effects of lncRNA RMRP, polypyrimidine tract-binding protein 1 (PTBP1), and AKT3 on MAECs stimulated with ox-LDL. RESULTS: Ox-LDL markedly reduced cell viability, increased proinflammatory factor levels, induced mitophagy, and reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in MAECs. Knockdown of lncRNA RMRP attenuated ox-LDL-induced inflammatory responses and mitophagy in MAECs. Knockdown of Methyltransferase-like 14 (METTL14) suppressed the expression of lncRNA RMRP through m6A modification in ox-LDL-treated MAECs. LncRNA RMRP enhanced AKT3 mRNA stability by interacting with PTBP1. LncRNA RMRP promoted ox-LDL-induced mitophagy by targeting AKT3 and stimulating the Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/AKT pathway in MAECs. CONCLUSION: METTL14 regulates the expression of lncRNA RMRP through m6A modification. Overexpressed lncRNA RMRP targets AKT3 by recruiting PTBP1, thus activating the PI3K/AKT pathway to mediate mitophagy and promote the progression of atherosclerosis.

title: Alzheimer's genetic risk factor CASS4 controls microglial focal adhesion biology and amyloidosis.
abstract: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified numerous Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk genes enriched in microglia, including Crk-associated substrate (Cas) scaffold protein family member 4 (CASS4), which encodes the adaptor protein CASS4. Despite its strong genetic association with AD, the role of CASS4 in disease remains poorly understood. Here, we show that full-body Cass4 deletion in 5xFAD mice increases amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, neuronal dystrophy, and cognitive deficits. Since microglia are the predominant brain-resident cells expressing Cass4, we investigated its role in microglial responses to Aβ pathology. Loss of CASS4 impaired microglial mobilization to Aβ plaques and reduced plaque compaction. Phosphoproteomic analysis of purified microglia revealed marked disruption of focal adhesion signaling following Cass4 deletion. Consistent with this, CASS4 deficiency abrogated in vivo microglial recruitment to injury and in vitro wound healing responses, two processes that are centrally orchestrated by focal adhesion biology. Together, these findings identify CASS4 as a critical regulator of microglial function and focal adhesion biology and suggest that CASS4 may represent a therapeutic target for AD.

title: Neuroprotectant development from small molecule inhibitors of CHOP/ATF4 expression.
abstract: Glaucoma is a neurodegenerative disease that is in urgent need of neuroprotective therapies. We previously revealed the critical role of neuronal endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress induced by optic nerve injury in glaucomatous neurodegeneration. We also demonstrated that modulation of the ATF4-CHOP branch of ER stress provides significant neuroprotection. Here, we present multiple new chemical series identified by high-throughput screening that inhibit ER stress-induced C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) expression. We perform a structure-activity relationship analysis of one "hit" compound and establish two analogs with potent activities on inhibiting the expression of CHOP and activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4). We further demonstrate their neuroprotective efficacy in two optic neuropathy models; in both models, they increase survival of retinal ganglion cell somata and axons and preserve visual function. Together, this proof-of-concept evidence establishes the new ER stress modulators as promising candidates for further drug development to provide neuroprotective therapy for glaucoma and other optic neuropathies, and potentially for diverse CNS axonopathies.

title: The deubiquitinase OTUD1 aggravated dopaminergic neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease model by promoting the degradation of Parkin.
abstract: Parkin plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease (PD). Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs), which reverse Parkin ubiquitination, are critical for maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. Although ovarian tumor protease deubiquitinase 1 (OTUD1) participates in various biological processes, its specific functions in PD and its regulation of Parkin remain unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that OTUD1 expression was significantly elevated in the nigrostriatal region of PD patients and MPTP-induced PD mice. Genetic ablation of OTUD1 markedly improved motor deficits and attenuated dopaminergic neuronal loss in PD models. Mechanistically, OTUD1 worsened mitochondrial dysfunction in PD models by negatively regulating Parkin protein levels. OTUD1 interacted with Parkin and selectively removed K27- and K33-linked polyubiquitin chains through its DUB activity, leading to Parkin degradation via the autophagic-lysosomal pathway. Our findings identify OTUD1 as a negative regulator of Parkin and reveal a mechanism linking deubiquitination to mitochondrial dysfunction in PD, which offers a novel potential therapeutic target for PD.

title: Trait-linked brainstem circuit resilience balances tau pathology-induced cellular vulnerability in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Although tau pathology correlates with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD), some individuals exhibit resilience by maintaining cognitive function. The mechanisms enabling this protection, particularly before widespread cortical degeneration occurs, remain elusive. Here, we identify a dynamic interplay between cellular vulnerability and circuit-level resilience that shapes cognitive outcomes in AD. Tau accumulation in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (EW) impairs attention by inducing hypoexcitability in CART+ neurons via Kcnma1 upregulation, a vulnerability predictive of future decline in both 3×Tg-AD mice and AD patients. Conversely, a subset of AD mice with heightened exploratory behavior activates a compensatory medial parabrachial (mPB)-EW circuit, mediated by substance P-Tacr1 signaling, which sustains CART+ neuron function and delays cognitive deterioration. These findings reveal resilience as an active state enabled by trait-linked circuit plasticity that balances cellular vulnerability, defining multilevel targets for early intervention.

title: Amygdala vulnerability in Pick disease with discrete frontotemporal dementia syndromes.
abstract: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration with tauopathy (FTLD-tau) typically manifests as either behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) or primary progressive aphasia (PPA). Tau pathology in FTLD-tau is characterized by predominantly three-repeat (3R) tau, as in Pick disease (PiD), or four-repeat (4R) tau species of corticobasal degeneration (CBD) and progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). FTLD-tau preferentially targets frontal and anterior temporal lobes, including the amygdala, contributing to severe neuropsychiatric symptoms. This study investigated whether bvFTD and PPA due to FTLD-tau exhibit distinct amygdalar histopathology and whether these patterns reflect their initially distinct clinical phenotypes, particularly in PiD. We examined 47 autopsy-confirmed FTLD-tau cases from the Northwestern Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Brain Bank using postmortem digital pathology analysis to quantify tau phosphorylation and HLA-DR immunoreactivity in the amygdala. In a subset of 19 PiD cases (10 bvFTD-PiD, 9 PPA-PiD), we assessed neuropsychiatric symptoms, tracked longitudinally using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory-Questionnaire (NPI-Q), and quantified neuronal and Pick body densities via unbiased stereology and neuronal sizes via digital pathology analysis. Across the FTLD-tau cohort, bvFTD exhibited greater amygdalar neuroinflammation than PPA, despite comparable tau burden. Interestingly, 3R cases also demonstrated higher levels of phosphorylated tau and MHC-II-positive microglia than 4R cases. In PiD, neuropsychiatric symptoms converged over time, with PPA cases evolving to show bvFTD-like symptoms with disease progression. BvFTD-PiD showed a trend toward greater MHC-II-positive microglia than PPA-PiD, despite similar neuronal size/density and Pick body burden. Increased HLA-DR immunoreactivity correlated positively with Pick body pathology. Neurons containing tau pathology (Pick cells) were notably larger than unaffected neurons, suggesting that early tau accumulation precedes overt neuronal degeneration. These findings underscore the potential role of neuroinflammation in shaping clinical phenotypes in FTLD and highlight the role of the amygdala in complex clinicopathologic relationships. Targeting neuroinflammatory processes may represent a viable therapeutic avenue for managing neuropsychiatric symptoms in tauopathies.

title: Altered developmental trajectories in neurodevelopmental disorders: mechanisms, human models and translational perspectives.
abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) are clinically and genetically heterogeneous conditions often studied through diagnostic categories, causal genes, synaptic dysfunction or end-stage phenotypes. Although these approaches remain essential, they do not fully capture the developmental nature of NDD pathophysiology. This review proposes a trajectory-first framework in which NDDs are interpreted as disorders of altered developmental progression. From this perspective, the key question is not only which gene, pathway, cell type, or synapse is affected, but when, where and how neurodevelopment begins to diverge. We discuss mechanisms of trajectory divergence, including altered developmental timing, cell-state and lineage disruption, selective cellular vulnerability, epigenetic and signaling dysregulation, cytoskeletal and morphogenetic abnormalities, synaptic maturation defects, excitability changes and network-level alterations. We then examine how human systems, including fetal and post-mortem atlases, iPSC-derived models, cortical organoids, assembloids, functional readouts and patient-level phenotypes, can be integrated to reconstruct developmental trajectories across biological scales. Representative NDD genes and syndromes illustrate that distinct divergence points may later converge on shared functional or clinical outcomes, including altered excitation/inhibition balance, abnormal network activity, epilepsy, language delay, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder features or motor dysfunction. Finally, we discuss limitations and perspectives for trajectory-based stratification and biomarker discovery. Rather than acting as static diagnostic readouts, future biomarkers should aim to capture developmental state, timing, divergence, convergence, compensation and response to intervention.

title: RLIM-associated neurodevelopmental disorders: From clinical spectrum to molecular mechanisms.
abstract: The E3 ubiquitin ligase RLIM (also known as RNF12) plays a central role in ubiquitin-dependent signaling pathways that regulate mammalian development. Missense variants in the RLIM gene cause Tønne-Kalscheuer syndrome (TOKAS), an X-linked recessive neurodevelopmental disorder affecting males, characterized by intellectual disability, developmental delay, and congenital abnormalities affecting the craniofacial, urogenital, ocular, and skeletal systems, as well as congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Additionally, RLIM duplications lead to a similar neurodevelopmental disorder, Chromosome Xq13 duplication syndrome. That both loss and gain of RLIM function produce overlapping neurodevelopmental phenotypes highlights the dosage sensitivity of this E3 ligase and points to its tightly regulated roles in human development. Despite an increasing number of reported cases, RLIM-associated disorders remain underdiagnosed and poorly understood, with no cure or targeted treatments, largely due to limited insight into the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying their pathogenesis. Here, we review current knowledge of RLIM biology across molecular, cellular, and genetic levels. We summarize the genetic basis, diagnostic criteria, and clinical spectrum of RLIM-associated disorders and integrate this with current understanding of RLIM-dependent ubiquitin signaling. By bringing together insights from biochemistry, cell signaling, and genetics, this review aimed to serve as a mechanistically informed reference for researchers and clinicians working on RLIM variants. We rank candidate RLIM substrates by the strength of the evidence linking them to disease. Finally, we discuss the key open questions that must be addressed to achieve a comprehensive cellular and molecular understanding of RLIM-associated disorders and thus lay the foundation for future therapeutic interventions.

overview: The E3 ubiquitin ligase RLIM (also known as RNF12) plays a central role in ubiquitin-dependent signaling pathways that regulate mammalian development.

title: Mitochondrial quality-control states in cadmium neurotoxicity: Adaptive clearance, disproportionate elimination and stalled flux.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) is a persistent environmental toxicant associated with neurological injury, but the role of mitophagy remains unresolved because increased pathway markers may indicate protective clearance, broad mitochondrial selection or incomplete downstream degradation. This review evaluates mitochondrial quality-control checkpoints in Cd-exposed neural systems, focusing on PINK1-Parkin, BNIP3L/NIX and autophagy-lysosome completion, and examines intervention evidence from puerarin, daidzein and ginsenoside Rg1. Three states are proposed as a conceptual synthesis: adaptive clearance, candidate disproportionate mitochondrial elimination and initiated but stalled flux. Protective PINK1- and BNIP3L-dependent activity has loss-of-function support, whereas selection-pathway engagement accompanied by mitochondrial loss is consistent with, but does not establish, disproportionate elimination because degradation and replacement have not been measured together. Cd also disrupts trafficking, autophagosome-lysosome fusion, lysosomal integrity and proteolysis, providing stronger evidence for incomplete bulk autophagic processing than for mitochondria-specific stalled flux. Among the compounds examined, puerarin has the broadest checkpoint coverage, largely from related cortical studies, linking reduced Cd burden and mitochondrial stress with pool preservation and improved bulk autophagic processing. Evidence for daidzein remains marker-limited, whereas Rg1 protects neuronal and glial endpoints without an established Cd-specific mitochondrial quality-control mechanism. This narrative, non-systematic synthesis is limited by potential selection bias, reliance on static markers, dominance of acute or high-dose exposure models, limited measurement of mitochondria-specific degradation and replacement, inadequate cell-type resolution and scarce independent replication. Resolving these states requires mitochondria-specific flux reporters, direct degradation and replacement indices, causal pathway perturbation and matched Cd and compound exposure. Therapeutic benefit is more likely to arise from restoring selective, proportionate and completed mitochondrial turnover balanced by replacement than from uniformly activating or suppressing mitophagy.

title: CNTN4: A Possible Candidate Gene for Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis in Autism Spectrum Disorders and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
abstract: The gut microbiota plays a significant role in autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), though findings vary substantially across studies. Using gut microbiome data from a genome-wide association study of 5,959 participants and summary statistics from 46,351 ASD and 55,374 ADHD cases, we conducted bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses with inverse variance weighting as the primary method. Reverse MR analysis assessed potential reverse causality. We annotated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with SNP-nexus to identify associated genes, followed by Gene Ontology (﻿GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses to characterize their functional roles. Seventeen gut microbial taxa showed causal associations with ASD risk, while 27 were linked to ADHD. Reverse MR analysis revealed associations between aSD and species Desulfovibrio piger as well as species Bacillus U, but no reverse causality was detected for ADHD. Biological annotation identified five novel conserved genes in host-microbiome interactions shared by ASD and ADHD, with CNTN4 emerging as a common candidate gene. These findings support a potential causal relationship between gut microbiota and ASD/ADHD risk while uncovering novel conserved genes implicated in host-microbiome interactions for both disorders.Lay AbstractDistinct gut microbiota profiles were observed in individuals with ADHD and ASD. Seventeen microbial species showed significant associations with ASD, while 27 were linked to ADHD. CNTN4 emerged as a potential candidate gene shared across both neurodevelopmental conditions and host-microbiome interactions.

title: Maternal microbiota shapes brain and neuroendocrine development in piglets.
abstract: The maternal microbiota plays a critical role in early-life development, yet how maternal microbiota exposure shapes cellular and neuroendocrine programs during mammalian development remains poorly understood. Here, leveraging germ-free (GF) and maternal microbiota transplantation (MMT) models, we generated an integrated multi-organ porcine atlas by combining multi-regional single-nucleus RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, bulk RNA sequencing of intestinal tissues, and metabolomics. Across five brain regions and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, we profiled 673,623 high-quality nuclei and revealed microbiota-dependent remodeling of neuronal and glial states across early postnatal developmental stages. MMT reshaped neuronal maturation programs, altered the distribution of immature neuronal states, and elicited region-specific transcriptional responses in glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons. MMT also reorganized neuron-glia interaction networks, accompanied by trends toward increased plasma glutamic acid and glutamine levels. Across the gut-brain-neuroendocrine axis, MMT was associated with coordinated remodeling of HPA-axis cellular communication, stress-response transcriptional programs, and immune signatures, together with reduced circulating cortisol levels. Integrated intestinal analyses revealed segment-specific transcriptional and metabolic remodeling, including alterations in tryptophan/indole-related metabolites and immune-associated pathways. Cross-species stratified linkage disequilibrium score regression further identified enrichment of human cognitive and neuropsychiatric trait-associated genetic signals within cell-type-specific gene signatures derived from microbiota-responsive porcine cell populations. Our study establishes a large-animal cellular atlas linking maternal microbiota-responsive remodeling across the brain, gut, and neuroendocrine axis, providing a translational framework for understanding how early-life microbial signals shape mammalian developmental physiology.

title: Activity-based proteomics discovery of deubiquitinating enzyme inhibitors with immunomodulatory activity.
abstract: Deubiquitinases (DUBs) play key roles in human pathologies, including cancer, infectious, autoimmune, and neurodegenerative diseases. The progress of potent and selective active site-targeting DUB inhibitors into clinical trials has demonstrated the therapeutic opportunities of such molecules; however, the shared catalytic geometry among DUB family members poses a challenge for achieving inhibitor selectivity. We describe a high-throughput, DUB-focused, activity-based proteomics workflow to identify new types of cysteine-reactive DUB inhibitors. We demonstrate the potential of αβ,α'β'-diepoxyketones (DEKs) and ubiquitin-derived covalently reacting alkynes as the first selective, cell-active compounds targeting USP47, OTUD7B (Cezanne), and USP5. These DUBs are reported to have critical roles in inflammasome formation, hypoxia, and viral replication, respectively. The identified compounds phenocopy these findings, demonstrating the tractability of these DUBs as immunotherapeutic targets.

title: Relaxin-2 protects synaptic integrity via hippocampal NLRP3-mTOR-autophagy pathways in an age-dependent Alzheimer-like model.
abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is associated with age-related synaptic degeneration, neuroinflammation, and impaired autophagy. The present study aimed to investigate the age-dependent neuroprotective effects of relaxin-2 (RLN2) in amyloid-beta 1-42 (Aβ1 - 42)-induced AD-like pathology and hypothesised that RLN2 would provide greater therapeutic benefit in young than aged mice. Young (3-4 months) and aged (12-14 months) mice were intracerebrally (i.c.) injected with amyloid-β (Aβ1 - 42) to develop an AD-like phenotype and treated with RLN2 or a control. Western blot analysis of hippocampal tissues was performed to assess the expression levels of ionised calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 (Iba1) (microglial activation marker), NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome components, and mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway activity. Neuroinflammation was determined by interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), while synaptic integrity was assessed by synaptophysin and PSD-95. The Morris Water Maze (MWM) and Novel Object Recognition (NOR) tests were used to measure cognitive and memory performance. Neuroinflammation markers IL-1β and TNF-α were significantly elevated in Aβ1 - 42-injected mice, with aged mice showing a greater increase than young mice. RLN2 treatment markedly reduced IL-1β and TNF-α levels in young mice, whereas the reduction was limited in aged mice. RLN2 treatment had a significant inhibitory effect on hippocampal NLRP3 signalling, reduced mTOR signalling, modulated autophagy-related protein expression, preserved synaptic proteins, and improved cognitive and memory performance (decrease in the MWM escape latency and increase in the NOR discrimination index). RLN2 was not effective in the aged mice, and there was persistent inflammatory activation, impaired autophagy, minimal improvement in synaptic recovery, and a moderate improvement in cognition. These findings suggest that RLN2 could be a potential therapeutic candidate for early-stage AD by targeting neuroinflammation, mTOR-mediated autophagy-related dysregulation, and synaptic loss, while also potentially providing a basis for age-based stratification of treatment responsiveness; however, further studies are required to determine its utility as a biomarker of treatment response or disease progression. Overall, RLN2 exerted neuro-protective effects in i.c. Aβ1 - 42-induced AD-like pathology in an age-dependent manner.

title: High-fat diet-induced MAFLD is associated with sleep architecture disruption via hippocampal neuroinflammation and bifurcated IRS-1/Akt/mTOR signaling in mice.
abstract: Epidemiological associations between metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) and sleep disturbances point to shared mechanisms, yet the underlying central pathways remain unexplored. We hypothesized that high-fat diet (HFD)-induced MAFLD disrupts sleep architecture via hippocampal neuroinflammation and dysregulation of the IRS-1/Akt/mTOR signaling axis. Male BALB/c mice were fed a control diet (CD) or a 60% HFD for 16 weeks to induce MAFLD. Sleep-wake architecture was assessed by 24-h EEG/EMG recordings. We evaluated hepatic steatosis, serum cytokines, hippocampal histology, and hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines. Hippocampal expression and phosphorylation of IRS-1 (Ser307), Akt (Ser473), and mTOR (Ser2448) were analyzed by Western blot. HFD-fed mice developed hepatic steatosis, elevated liver enzymes, and increased serum tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β). These mice exhibited reduced non‑rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep duration, severe sleep fragmentation (reflected by increased bout numbers and shorter mean bout durations), and diminished NREM sleep delta power. Cosinor analysis revealed a dampened circadian rhythm of NREM sleep delta power. In the hippocampus, HFD induced neuronal injury, elevated TNF-α and IL-1β levels, accompanied by a bifurcated signaling profile: increased p-IRS-1 (Ser307), decreased p-Akt (Ser473), and elevated p-mTOR (Ser2448). Our findings identify a putative liver-hippocampus-sleep axis in which MAFLD-driven systemic inflammation and hippocampal IRS-1/Akt/mTOR dysregulation are associated with profound sleep disruption, providing a framework for future mechanistic validation. Targeting this axis may offer new therapeutic strategies for sleep disorders in MAFLD.

title: Analysis of Urolithin A's regulation of microglial inflammation and autophagy in herpes simplex encephalitis via modulating the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway through network pharmacology.
abstract: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is severe central nervous system inflammation triggered by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). Urolithin A (UA), an intestinal flora-derived metabolite from dietary ellagitannins, possesses anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and autophagy-regulating properties, yet its regulatory function on microglia during HSE remains unclear. HSV-1-infected BV2 mouse microglia were used as an in vitro HSE model. CCK-8 was applied to detect cell viability; ELISA measured inflammatory cytokine secretion; qRT-PCR and flow cytometry assessed M1 microglial polarization; western blot tested autophagy-associated protein expression. Network pharmacology screened potential UA targets, and rescue assays validated the involvement of the PI3K/AKT pathway. UA exerted no obvious cytotoxicity against BV2 cells within 0-20 µM and restored viability of HSV-1-damaged BV2 cells. It reduced TNF-α, IL-6 and IFN-β release, downregulated M1 markers (iNOS, TNF-α) and CD86-positive cell proportion, and suppressed excessive autophagy via decreasing LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and elevating p62 expression. Network pharmacology identified Akt1 as the core target linked to the PI3K/AKT pathway. Rescue tests revealed that PI3K/AKT activation abolished UA's regulatory effects. In summary, UA alleviates HSV-1-induced microglial inflammatory injury by inhibiting PI3K/AKT overactivation, M1 polarization and abnormal autophagy.

title: Microglial NUS1 deficiency drives dopaminergic neurodegeneration through intercellular iron dysregulation in Parkinson's disease models.
abstract: The selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. NUS1, which encodes neurite outgrowth inhibitor-B receptor (NgBR), was recently identified as a PD risk gene. Here we show that NgBR is highly expressed in microglia, where its deficiency drives progressive PD-like motor deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration via the LCN2-SLC22A17 iron-transport axis in mice. NgBR deficiency in mouse and human microglia triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress and PERK-ATF4-NUPR1 signaling, which preferentially induces LCN2-mediated iron efflux over cytokine release. Subsequently, microglia-derived iron-loaded Holo-LCN2, but not iron-free Apo-LCN2, is internalized by SLC22A17, a receptor highly expressed in dopaminergic neurons, leading to iron overload and ferroptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of LCN2-SLC22A17 axis or ferroptosis alleviated dopaminergic neuron loss and PD-like symptoms caused by microglial NgBR deficiency in vitro and in vivo. Our findings identify disrupted intercellular iron homeostasis as a pathological driver of PD and highlight the LCN2-SLC22A17 axis as a potential therapeutic target.

title: TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis-induced microglial senescence underlies benzo[a]pyrene-associated Parkinson's disease-like lesions.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. Accumulating evidence has linked environmental polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), with benzo[a]pyrene (B[a]P) as a representative ubiquitous member, to elevated PD risk and disease pathogenesis. The present study aimed to investigate whether B[a]P can trigger typical PD-like lesions in mice, and further dissects the functional role of microglial senescence as well as its underlying regulatory mechanism, using complementary systems in vivo mouse model and in vitro BV2 microglia cell. Behavioral assessments revealed that B[a]P exposure induced significant, dose-dependent impairments in motor coordination and cognitive function compared with the control group. Moreover, the degree of functional impairments measured in the high-dose B[a]P group was comparable to that observed in the MPTP positive-control group. Following B[a]P treatment, brain-resident microglia cells exhibited signs of cell senescence, as evidenced by typical ultrastructural alterations, increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity, and elevated expression of the core senescence markers p16, p21, and p53 proteins. Consistent with these in vivo observations, B[a]P was confirmed to also induce cell cycle arrest in cultured BV2 microglia cells. This pro-senescent effect was significnatly attenuated by Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) overexpression, whereas it was markedly exacerbated following TREM2 knockout. Subsequent experiments further validated that insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), as a direct downstream effector regulated by TREM2, is functionally required for B[a]P-triggered microglial senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that B[a]P exposure can induce PD-like lesions and microglial senescence, and which is primarily mediated via the TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis.
