title: Named neurons of the nervous system: a historical narrative review of discovery, function, and legacy.
abstract: Many currently applied terms in neuroanatomy are rooted in important historical breakthroughs. Some discoveries become timeless, some evolve as knowledge advances, and others disappear into history before being rediscovered by a later generation. Purkinje cells, Betz cells, Golgi cells, Renshaw cells, and Onuf's nucleus are spoken of so routinely that their eponymous significance is not always immediately apparent. Yet each one reflects a moment of curiosity, a painstaking observation under a microscope, an inspired technical breakthrough, or, at times, an intense scientific rivalry. The history of named neurons mirrors the history of neuroscience. As microscopy and histological staining techniques improved, anatomists were able to see structures that had previously been invisible, transforming the nervous system from an indistinct mass into an intricate landscape of specialized cells. Some discoveries, such as Golgi's staining method and Cajal's neuron doctrine, reshaped biology forever (Golgi, 1873; Ramón y Cajal, 1906). Others were slower to be recognized: von Economo neurons, for example, were described, forgotten for nearly seven decades, and only later recognized as a distinct neuronal population (Betz, 1881, as cited in Butti et al. 2013; von Economo, 1926; Nimchinsky et al. 1999). This review follows these remarkable journeys, exploring neurons named after their discoverers alongside those named for their appearance or function, including chandelier cells, place cells, mirror neurons, and concept cells. Together, they demonstrate the depth of many familiar names in neuroanatomy-not merely as descriptive labels, but also as windows into the history, ingenuity, and enduring curiosity that continues to shape modern neuroscience.

title: Arhgef1 Deletion Disrupts Early Cortical Neurogenesis via PAK1 Overactivation and Causes Motor Dysfunction in Adulthood.
abstract: Precise regulation of early cortical development is essential for the establishment of normal brain function, and its disruption can contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). Impaired motor function is a prominent early manifestation of various NDDs, yet the mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identified ARHGEF1, a Rho family guanine nucleotide exchange factor highly expressed during early corticogenesis, as a novel regulator in embryonic cortical neurogenesis and adult motor function. By Emx1-Cre-mediated forebrain deletion of Arhgef1 in mice (Arhgef1 cKO mice), early cortical neurogenesis is specifically disrupted, leading to reduced deep-layer cortical neurons. Mechanistically, Arhgef1 deficiency overactivates RAC1/CDC42-PAK1-Cofilin signaling in early cortical development, whereas pharmacological PAK1 inhibition within this critical window rescues the genesis of deep-layer cortical neurons. Importantly, Arhgef1 cKO mice exhibit remarkable motor learning and coordination deficits in adulthood, accompanied by altered neuronal morphology in the motor cortex and impaired neuronal activities in motor circuits. In all, we elucidate a critical developmental window when ARHGEF1 governs corticogenesis via negatively regulates PAK1-dependent pathway and further reveal an important role for ARHGEF1 in maintaining normal motor function in adulthood.

title: Adult ADHD, PARK2 copy number variations and the blood-brain barrier: Culture duration-dependent metabolic alterations in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived in vitro models.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a multifactorial neurodevelopmental disorder in which PARK2 copy number variations (CNVs) constitute a rare genetic risk factor. PARK2 encodes parkin, a key regulator of mitochondrial quality control. Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in ADHD pathophysiology and can contribute to blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption. As BBB disruption remains insufficiently understood in ADHD, this study investigated whether adult ADHD and PARK2 CNVs are accompanied by alterations in BBB phenotype, mitochondrial properties, and cellular metabolism. METHODS: Brain capillary endothelial-like cells (BCECs) were generated using 10 donor-specific human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines from adults with ADHD carrying PARK2 CNVs, alongside PARK2 wild type adults with and without ADHD. BCECs were analyzed at the end of differentiation (day 10) and after prolonged culture (day 17) to assess group-associated phenotypes and culture duration-dependent differences. RESULTS: Across all groups, BCECs showed brain endothelial marker expression, high transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER), and low sodium fluorescein (NaFl) permeability at day 10. After prolonged culture, NaFl permeability remained low, whereas TEER-based barrier integrity declined. Prolonged culture of BCECs reduced glycolytic ATP production rates while increasing mitochondrial ATP production and its relative contribution to total ATP production, reflecting a metabolic shift from glycolysis toward oxidative phosphorylation. Despite decreased total ATP production after prolonged culture, cellular energy status was largely preserved, alongside overall lower intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitochondrial membrane potential. At day 10, BCECs from ADHD donors carrying PARK2 duplications displayed greater mitochondrial abundance, the highest basal and oxidative stress-induced intracellular ROS levels, and reduced TEER-based barrier integrity, while at day 17, BCECs from ADHD donors with PARK2 deletions exhibited the least glycolysis-dependent ATP production profile, although absolute mitochondrial ATP production remained comparable between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Prolonged culture was associated with broad, ADHD- and PARK2 genotype-independent metabolic remodeling, whereas mitochondrial and metabolic alterations associated with ADHD and PARK2 CNVs were overall small. This study identifies culture duration as a critical parameter for the characterization of hiPSC-derived BBB in vitro models and supports the feasibility of using donor-specific BCECs at the end of differentiation to investigate BBB-associated mechanisms in adult ADHD and PARK2 CNVs.

title: Characteristics of visual search and prefrontal brain activity in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: functional near-infrared spectroscopy study.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The term 'visual search' (VS) is used to describe behaviors such as finding a desired item while shopping or looking for a room key. These behaviors are important in everyday life. Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have been reported to experience difficulties with VS. However, the characteristics of VS and the associated brain activity remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated these characteristics in detail using a measurement method that combined VS tasks with brain function measurements. METHODS: Twenty-one individuals with ASD and 42 typically developing (TD) individuals, matched for age and visual intelligence, participated in this study. The characteristics of VS were evaluated using two types of cancellation tasks: structured and random arrays. We evaluated VS performance using various measurements, including the rate of intersections and the best r, which reflect systematicity and directional constancy. We measured brain activity using functional near-infrared spectroscopy in the prefrontal cortex (PFC). RESULTS: The ASD group had a significantly higher rate of intersections and a significantly lower best r than the TD group. The right PFC activity was significantly higher than the activity in other PFC regions during the random array task in the TD group. Additionally, the TD group exhibited significantly higher right PFC activity than the ASD group. CONCLUSION: These results suggest that VS in individuals with ASD is characterized by inconsistent search direction and disorganization and that patterns of PFC brain activity during VS may also differ from those observed in TD individuals.

title: Macamide B alleviates neuronal pyroptosis in spinal cord injury by activating acid ceramidase to inhibit lysosome membrane permeabilization.
abstract: Spinal cord injury is a devastating neurological disorder that causes severe and persistent functional deficits, for which effective pharmacological treatments remain limited. Acid ceramidase is a key lysosomal hydrolase involved in sphingolipid metabolism and has been implicated in cellular homeostasis and central nervous system disorders. However, its role in lysosomal membrane permeabilization and autophagic flux following spinal cord injury remains unclear. In this study, virtual screening identified macamide B as a potential activator of acid ceramidase, and its neuroprotective effects and underlying mechanisms were investigated in a mouse model of spinal cord injury. We found that macamide B treatment significantly reduced glial scar formation and motor neuron loss, thereby improving functional recovery after spinal cord injury. Moreover, macamide B suppressed neuronal pyroptosis and restored impaired autophagic flux associated with lysosomal membrane permeabilization. Mechanistically, macamide B activated acid ceramidase through the extracellular signal-regulated kinase/mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway, thereby alleviating lysosomal membrane permeabilization and restoring autophagic flux, ultimately attenuating neuronal pyroptosis and neuronal loss. Collectively, these findings reveal an extracellular signal-regulated kinase/mitogen-activated protein kinase/acid ceramidase-mediated mechanism underlying the neuroprotective effects of macamide B after spinal cord injury and suggest that pharmacological activation of acid ceramidase may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for promoting neurological recovery following spinal cord injury.

title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. We propose that loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function disrupts postsynaptic endosome positioning, leading to aberrant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog-mediated F-actin remodeling, pathological enhancement of excitatory postsynaptic densities, excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor targeting, and increased vulnerability to excitotoxicity.

title: From Cell to Circuit: Altered Functional Network Topology in iPSC-derived Neuronal Circuits in Major Depressive Disorder.
abstract: The functional organization of brain networks relies on a delicate balance between segregation and integration, which supports both localized neural processing and global information exchange. While numerous whole-brain imaging studies have linked disruptions in this balanced topology to Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), it remains unclear whether such macroscale alterations are reflected in neuronal circuit dynamics at the cellular level. In this study, we investigated whether neuronal networks derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) of nine MDD patients display a distinct functional topology compared to nine matched controls. We obtained skin biopsies from all participants, cultivated fibroblasts, and reprogrammed these into hiPSCs. We then differentiated hiPSCs into neural progenitor cells (NPCs), which we later developed into neurons. We recorded spontaneous activity in the derived neuronal networks using calcium imaging, and applied graph theory analysis to quantify differences in functional topology between groups. We observed a significant decrease in the clustering coefficient and average node degree in MDD-derived neural networks. Furthermore, global efficiency showed a downward trend across varying thresholds and network sizes in patient-derived lines. Together, these findings demonstrate diminished segregation and reduced overall nodal connectivity in MDD-derived neural networks. This suggests that a predisposition for less efficient functional topology exists in depression at the microscale, highlighting the utility of hiPSC technology in modeling cellular disease mechanisms and exploring potential cellular correlates of network-level phenomena reported in depression.

title: Constructing functional neural circuits to model amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons. Recent advances in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids offer an innovative platform to model amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in a human-specific context. These three-dimensional organoid systems allow for the study of neuronal circuit-level dysfunction, which is central to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis pathogenesis, by incorporating multiple neuronal subtypes and supporting glial populations. In particular, the integration of region-specific brain organoids into assembloid models has enabled the reconstruction of functional long-range projections and cortico-motor circuits, closely resembling human neural connectivity. This review summarizes the generation and application of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis research, with a focus on the reconstruction of neural circuits, multi-omics profiling, and functional assays. We also discuss how organoid systems can be leveraged for drug discovery and personalized medicine in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, highlighting their potential to unveil human-specific disease mechanisms. Lastly, we address the current challenges and future directions for improving the physiological relevance of organoid models in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis research.

title: Exosomes in remote ischemic preconditioning-mediated organ protection: Molecular mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Remote ischemic preconditioning (RIPC) is an endogenous protective strategy that confers resistance against sustained ischemia-reperfusion injury in distant organs. RIPC induces protective responses through complex neuronal, humoral, and systemic signaling pathways. Increasing evidence suggests that exosomes may serve as important mediators of humoral inter-organ communication during RIPC. Exosomes are small extracellular vesicles released by donor cells that transport biologically active molecules, including lipids, proteins, messenger RNAs, and microRNAs, to recipient cells, thereby modulating cellular responses to injury. Emerging evidence indicates that RIPC-associated exosomes and their molecular cargo contribute to protection against ischemia-reperfusion injury in organs such as the heart, brain, kidney, and spinal cord. Several exosomal molecules, including miRNAs, HSP90, HIF-1α, and NOX2, have been implicated in the regulation of cellular pathways associated with inflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, mitochondrial function, and tissue survival. In particular, alterations in exosomal miRNAs and protein and metabolite profiles following RIPC suggest that exosomes may participate in the transmission of protective signals from remote ischemic tissues to target organs. The therapeutic potential of exosomes is further supported by their ability to transport multiple bioactive molecules and their potential application as biomarkers or delivery vehicles for therapeutic cargo. However, the specific exosomal components responsible for RIPC-mediated protection and their causal contribution to inter-organ signaling remain to be fully established. Therefore, the present review summarizes the emerging evidence on the role of exosomes in RIPC-mediated organ protection, with particular emphasis on cardiovascular and cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury, the molecular cargo involved, underlying protective mechanisms, and their potential therapeutic and translational applications.

title: Digital twin control framework uncovers individualized cross-scale links between functional connectivity deviations, communication impairment, and molecular mechanisms in autism.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. METHODS: We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyzes and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. RESULTS: The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting it is associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.

title: Clinical, immunological and metabolic features and gut-brain axis markers in children with autism spectrum disorder and TORCH-associated central nervous system involvement.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) have heterogeneous etiologies, with TORCH infections potentially contributing to neurodevelopmental disruption through central nervous system injury and gut-brain axis dysfunction. METHODS: A prospective comparative study enrolled 280 children aged 3-10 years with ASD: 112 with TORCH-associated central nervous system (CNS) involvement (main group) and 168 with idiopathic ASD (comparison group), alongside 25 healthy controls. Assessments included clinical/neurological features, autism severity, gastrointestinal symptoms, pro-inflammatory cytokines, metabolic markers, neuron-specific enolase (NSE), fecal zonulin, and brain MRI. TORCH pathogens were detected by PCR from saliva samples. RESULTS: TORCH-associated ASD exhibited a more severe phenotype with greater frequencies of delayed speech, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, hyperactivity, emotional-behavioral dysregulation, epileptiform manifestations, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Severe ASD was significantly more common in the TORCH group. Laboratory analyses revealed significantly elevated interleukin-1β, interleukin-8, tumor necrosis factor alpha, homocysteine, ammonia, uric acid, NSE, and fecal zonulin, with reduced folate. Fecal zonulin was positively correlated with inflammatory markers and neuron-specific enolase. MRI more frequently demonstrated periventricular gliosis, ventriculomegaly, subependymal abnormalities, and diffuse residual organic changes. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, ASD with clinical evidence of TORCH-associated CNS involvement was associated with greater clinical severity and higher serum inflammatory, metabolic, neuronal-injury, fecal-zonulin, and structural MRI measures than ASD without such evidence. The cross-sectional design and limitations of salivary PCR preclude causal attribution to TORCH infection.

title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

title: Zinc activates autophagy by regulating HDAC6 expression following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
abstract: Intracellular zinc accumulation and excessive autophagy have been reported to contribute to neuronal death following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R). Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), which contains a zinc-dependent active site, is closely associated with autophagy. However, the relationship between zinc, HDAC6 and autophagy following cerebral I/R remains unclear. In this study, we aim to investigate whether ischemia-induced zinc accumulation activates autophagy through HDAC6. Rats were treated with zinc chelator, autophagy activator/inhibitor or HDAC6 inhibitor during a 90-minute middle cerebral artery occlusion. Infarct volume, neurological deficits, protein expression, and the colocalization of HDAC6, Beclin1, and zinc in neurons were evaluated. Our results demonstrate that beclin1 expression was significantly increased after cerebral I/R and this elevation was markedly attenuated by zinc chelation. Notably, reactivation of autophagy with rapamycin significantly, though not completely, diminished TPEN-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting that zinc-induced autophagy is an important contributor to neuronal injury following cerebral I/R. Moreover, immunofluorescence revealed that HDAC6 was colocalized with Beclin1 in the penumbra of ischemic rats, and inhibition of HDAC6 reduced Beclin1 expression and alleviated brain injury. Molecular docking analysis suggested a potential interaction between HDAC6 and α-tubulin, which may influence autophagy by regulating microtubule stability and autophagosome transport. Furthermore, chelating zinc decreased HDAC6 expression, while HDAC6 inhibition did not influence zinc levels, demonstrating that zinc acts upstream of HDAC6. In conclusion, our findings identify a novel zinc-HDAC6-autophagy signaling axis underlying neuronal injury following cerebral I/R, suggesting that targeting zinc homeostasis or HDAC6 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy.

title: Are 5 G radiofrequency electromagnetic fields and PARP1 interfering with the development of human iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons?
abstract: The rapid expansion of wireless technologies has increased exposure to radiofrequency electromagnetic fields (RF-EMF), with evolving frequencies and network configurations complicating assessment of potential health risks. Although no conclusive evidence links RF-EMF exposure to adverse health outcomes, including neurodevelopmental disorders or neurodegeneration, some studies suggest possible effects on cognitive functions. In this study, we address the role of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1), a protein involved in neuronal development and neurodegeneration, and evaluate potential effects of RF-EMF. Dopaminergic neurons derived from wild-type (WT) and PARP1-knockout (KO) human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) were exposed to RF-EMF during differentiation. PARP1 levels in WT cells decreased between differentiation and maturation, supporting its role during early neuronal development. The absence of PARP1 resulted in a prominent increase in dopaminergic phenotype at maturation when compared to differentiation, while protein levels of the dopaminergic progenitor marker decreased. Neuronal maturity was unaffected by genotype, while increased expression of the presynaptic marker synaptophysin suggests enhanced synaptic function in PARP1-KO cells compared to WT cells. Neuronal activity was developing over time in both WT and PARP1-KO cells. However, PARP1 deficiency was associated with selective changes in spike timing and burst-related properties, particularly at early and late differentiation stages. RF-EMF exposure did not alter the neuronal phenotype, development, synaptic integrity, or electrical activity in either genotype. Proteomic analysis further supports that genotype-dependent differences were greater than any RF-EMF-related exposure effects. Future studies should assess RF-EMF exposure at later developmental stages and investigate PARP1 function in disease-relevant models. In conclusion, PARP1 absence was associated with an enhanced dopaminergic phenotype, indicating that PARP1 may influence neuronal differentiation, maturation, and synaptic plasticity. Electrical activity increased with maturation time, consistent with progressive functional development of the neuronal culture. Overall, neuronal development was predominantly influenced by the genotype, whereas RF-EMF exposure produced only transient effects on the dopaminergic phenotype. Evidence of a genotype-dependent response to RF-EMF exposure was observed only for SYP and mTOR.

title: Characterization of human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)- derived Kidney Organoids as a Platform to Assess Drug-Induced Nephrotoxicity.
abstract: Drug inducted nephrotoxicity is a major cause of withdrawal of Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved drugs. Animal models and 2D cell culture approaches do not faithfully replicate the structure and drug response associated with human renal tissues. Therefore, the goal of this study is to develop 3D organoid-based models of the kidney to provide a physiologically relevant platform to screen drugs for potential nephrotoxicity. In this study, kidney organoids were created using a process that involves mesodermal induction, organoid , and kidney differentiation. Immunofluorescence imaging was used to profile and quantitatively assess the presence of cells associated with the kidney including endothelial cells and renal tubular cells. Multicellular kidney organoids were then exposed to increasing concentrations (25-800 µM) of four nephrotoxic agents of varying levels of toxicity: cisplatin, gentamicin, dexamethasone, and probenecid. Cisplatin and gentamicin represent high toxicity drugs whereas, dexamethasone and probenecid represent low toxicity drugs. Cellular injury was assessed via evaluation of cell death. Our results show that drug-treated organoids exhibit dose-dependent increases in cell death with significant cell death associated with high toxicity drugs. These findings provide preliminary support for kidney organoids as valuable platforms to study nephrotoxic injury. Further optimization of both organoid maturation and toxicity assays can potentially enhance the reliability and physiological relevance of kidney organoid-based in-vitro platforms for nephrotoxicity testing.

title: 53BP1 as a cofactor in the activation of the p53-family transcriptional program: A correlative multimodal microscopy approach.
abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M3.I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M3.I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family-dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M3.I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.

title: Chronic thoracic aortitis versus primary medial degeneration in ascending aorta: a digital morphometric analysis of aortic layers remodelling.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic aortitis (CA) represents a diverse group of inflammatory conditions often diagnosed incidentally in ascending aorta biopsies. While the 2015 and 2016 Consensus Statements on the surgical pathology of the aorta provide standardised histological classifications, data quantifying structural remodelling within individual aortic layers remain limited. Furthermore, distinguishing CA from primary non-inflammatory medial degeneration (MD) can be challenging, particularly when inflammation is sparse or burnt out, and secondary degenerative changes predominate. We aimed to compare morphological changes in CA and MD aneurysms and apply digital image analysis to quantify aortic wall layers. METHODS: Retrospective histological analysis was performed on 63 ascending aortic specimens: CA (n=21), MD (n=21), and autopsy controls (n=21). Digitised elastic-stained sections were analysed using QuPath software to measure the thickness and cross-sectional area of the intima (I), media (M), and adventitia (A). Overall MD scores (i.e., summaries of each MD grade component) were evaluated. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis based on binary logistic regression models. RESULTS: CA demonstrated a profound architectural shift, characterised by medial thinning alongside marked intimal and adventitial expansion, resulting in significantly lower M/(I+A) thickness and area ratios compared with MD and controls (p <0.001). CA specimens also exhibited the most severe secondary degenerative changes, with significantly higher overall MD scores (median: 15 vs. 8; p < 0.001). ROC curve analysis revealed diagnostic utility of both the M/(I+A) thickness ratio (AUC = 0.964) and the M/(I+A) area ratio (AUC = 0.955) for identifying CA. A multivariable model combining the overall MD score with the M/(I+A) thickness ratio achieved an AUC of 0.971 (accuracy 88.1%), whereas combining it with the M/(I+A) area ratio yielded an AUC of 0.968 (accuracy 90.5%). CONCLUSION: Digital morphometric analysis provides a reproducible and feasible method for quantifying structural remodelling in chronic aortitis. Changes in the proportions of the aortic layers, specifically intimal and adventitial expansion combined with medial thinning and severe secondary medial degeneration, can facilitate accurate differentiation of aortic wall pathologies, particularly in cases with sparse inflammation.

title: The spectrum within the spectrum: Neural heterogeneity in autism.
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.

title: Glial lipid reprogramming in brain aging: Lipid identity, organelle stress, and redox vulnerability.
abstract: Brain aging is accompanied by progressive glial dysfunction, impaired metabolic adaptation, oxidative stress, and increased susceptibility to neurodegenerative disease. Although many studies of lipid metabolism in aging and neurodegeneration emphasize lipid abundance, lipid amount alone cannot explain why glia become redox-vulnerable. This review advances a chemistry-resolved integrative framework in which glial lipid reprogramming is understood through aging- and disease-associated changes in lipid identity, composition, oxidation state, storage form, subcellular localization, and lipid-mediated signaling. We discuss evidence from aged brain tissue, human neurodegenerative disease, iPSC-derived glial systems, and mouse models showing that altered lipid handling in microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells reshapes phagocytosis, inflammatory signaling, myelin processing, astrocytic metabolic support, and neuronal injury. We emphasize that acyl-chain saturation, head-group structure, oxidized lipid species, neutral lipid storage, plasmalogen-dependent redox buffering, peroxisomal lipid metabolism, and compartmental distribution determine how lipids regulate receptor engagement, lipid-droplet dynamics, lysosomal stress, mitochondrial function, ferroptotic susceptibility, and inflammatory redox signaling. Importantly, glial lipid reprogramming is further shaped by extracellular vesicle-mediated neuron-glia communication, regional lipid heterogeneity, and sex-dependent modifiers of glial metabolism. Oxidative stress therefore reflects the convergence of polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA)-enriched membranes, oxidized phospholipids, oxysterols, ceramide accumulation, plasmalogen loss, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, lysosomal iron release, peroxisomal dysfunction, and declining glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), GTP cyclohydrolase 1-tetrahydrobiopterin (GCH1-BH4), and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2)-dependent protective systems. Finally, we discuss lipid-centered therapeutic opportunities targeting cholesterol efflux, apolipoprotein E (APOE) lipidation, lipid-droplet metabolism, sphingolipid pathways, lipid peroxide defense, plasmalogen support, extracellular vesicle biology, and lipid-based delivery systems. By shifting the focus from lipid accumulation to lipid identity, compartmental handling, and biological context, this review synthesizes glial lipid reprogramming as an integrative framework linking brain aging to redox-sensitive neurodegeneration.

title: Conserved SINE and lineage-variable LINE-1 depletion at neurodevelopmental disorder promoters.
abstract: Developmental genes lie in transposon-poor regions, but whether that deficit is a conserved property of the promoters themselves remains unmeasured. Transposable element frequency was compared at neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) promoters (TSS ±2 kb) in seven primates and two outgroups, contrasting a curated NDD gene set (SFARI and ClinGen; [Formula: see text]) with brain-expressed housekeeping genes ([Formula: see text]). Alu depletion was significant in every primate ([Formula: see text] to [Formula: see text]), including the mouse lemur at 70 Mya. Mouse B1 and B2, SINEs amplified independently of primate Alu, each showed the deficit; the AT-biased Can-SINEs of dog did not. LINE-1 depletion was weak against housekeeping promoters but comparable to or deeper than the SINEs against the genome baseline, and more lineage-variable. The signal survived permutation testing, CpG and GC stratification, and gene-density and recombination controls. It persisted for alignment-defined rather than annotation-defined promoter windows, and against each genome's own baseline in seven of nine, marmoset and dog excepted; the squirrel monkey showed no such exception. Against human controls matched on constraint, brain expression and GC it narrowed but persisted ([Formula: see text]); Alu density does not otherwise track constraint. Windows away from the start site separate two components: the surrounding 250 kb is itself Alu-poor, and a promoter-proximal deficit survives normalisation to it. Depleted promoters coincided with active cis-regulatory elements, preferentially fetal-brain ones. Low promoter SINE content is thus an old feature of NDD-associated loci; whether the elements were never inserted or inserted and later lost is unresolved.

title: Attention load modulates functional brain connectivity reorganization in children with high autistic traits: Evidence from phase and amplitude coupling metrics.
abstract: Whether emotional processing difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) stem from deficits in recognizing emotional stimuli or from limitations in flexibly reorganizing brain networks under increasing cognitive demands remains an open question. To our knowledge, this study is among the first to investigate the effects of graded attentional load (low/moderate/high) on EEG-based functional connectivity and brain network organization during task-irrelevant emotional prosody processing in children with high autistic traits (n = 31), by integrating phase-based (iPLV, wPLI) and amplitude-based (AEC) metrics together with graph-theoretic indices within a unified analytic framework. Connectivity matrices from a sliding-window approach were decomposed into edge-level, distributional, and graph-theoretic features and load-dependent changes in connectivity were assessed with statistical analyzes and classification models. The results suggested that attentional load did not uniformly increase or decrease connectivity but rather produced a multi-layered pattern of reorganization that varied as a function of frequency band, connectivity metric, and network topology. Phase-based connectivity in the beta band was decreased with increasing load, while amplitude envelope coupling (AEC) in the theta and alpha bands was increased under high load. This dual-mechanism pattern was most pronounced under the high-load condition, which yielded the greatest number of nominally significant features (uncorrected p < 0.05; none survived FDR correction), the largest theta-AEC effect size (Kendall's W up to 0.22), and the best-performing classification model among those tested (accuracy = 72.6%, F1 = 0.725, AUC = 0.764). In conclusion, this exploratory study suggests that, in children with high autistic traits, increasing cognitive demands may be associated with band-specific network reorganization characterized by attenuated phase-based coordination alongside enhanced amplitude-based coupling; these patterns did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, have not been compared with those of typically developed children, and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. If replicated, such findings could eventually inform how environmental stimulation and cognitive load are structured in special education settings.

title: Opposing Patterns of the Histone Variant MacroH2A1.1 in Fmr1 Knockout and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J Mouse Models of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity, wherein genetic and idiopathic forms may converge on shared core phenotypes through divergent molecular pathways. The histone variant macroH2A1.1, implicated in chromatin repression and DNA repair, has been linked to behavioral alterations opposite to core ASD features when depleted systemically. However, its regional and cell-type-specific regulation in genetic versus idiopathic ASD models remains unclear. We investigated macroH2A1.1 expression across the dorsal striatum, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex in Fmr1 knockout (Fragile X syndrome model) and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J (idiopathic ASD model) mice. Quantitative PCR and imaging analyses revealed opposing patterns: BTBR mice showed region-specific mRNA downregulation and increased strongly stained macroH2A1.1-positive nuclei, whereas Fmr1 knockout mice exhibited reduced strong staining with increased weak staining, specific to neurons and not astrocytes, independent of significant mRNA changes. Bulk RNA-seq meta-analysis and pseudobulk single-cell transcriptomics further identified pathway-level enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, chromatin remodeling, and transcriptional repression functional gene sets in unmatched public datasets (BTBR striatum; FXS hippocampus and cortex), with pronounced neuron-astrocyte divergence in Fmr1 knockout cortex. These findings underscore distinct epigenetic regulatory mechanisms in genetic and idiopathic ASD models.
authors: Ivanov MN, Mladenov A, Tsoneva DK, Napoli A, Mazza T, Tonchev AB, Coppola I, Chiodi V, Tartaglione AM, Vinciguerra M
overview: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity, wherein genetic and idiopathic forms may converge on shared core phenotypes through divergent molecular pathways.
main: Quantitative PCR and imaging analyses revealed opposing patterns: BTBR mice showed region-specific mRNA downregulation and increased strongly stained macroH2A1.1-positive nuclei, whereas Fmr1 knockout mice exhibited reduced strong staining with increased weak staining, specific to neurons and not astrocytes, independent of significant mRNA changes.

title: BHLHE22 monoallelic and biallelic variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with agenesis of the corpus callosum, intellectual disability, abnormal muscle tone and movement abnormalities.
abstract: BACKGROUND: BHLHE22 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor (bHLH) expressed exclusively in the retina and central nervous system (CNS), and functions as an important regulator of neuronal differentiation. However, BHLHE22 has not yet been associated with a Mendelian neurodevelopmental or neurological disorder. METHODS: Fifteen individuals from thirteen unrelated families carrying BHLHE22 variants identified by exome sequencing were collected through an international collaboration. RESULTS: De novo missense variants located in the highly conserved helix-loop-helix domain of the protein were found in six individuals, and one recurrent homozygous frameshift variant, NP_689627.1:p.Gly74AlafsTer18, was found in nine individuals. Frequent clinical features include absent or limited speech (10/13), delayed or impaired motor abilities (11/13), intellectual disability (9/12), partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum (12/15), involuntary movements and/or stereotypies (11/13), and abnormal muscle tone (13/13), depending on data availability. Two individuals developed spastic paraplegia, without intellectual disability (ID) or callosal anomalies. One individual had moderate developmental delay and ID, but without callosal anomalies. CONCLUSION: Collectively, our data establish BHLHE22 as a previously unrecognized neurodevelopmental disease gene. Disruption of BHLHE22, through either dominant or recessive variants, results in a distinct syndrome characterized by abnormalities in brain development, cognition, tone, and movement.

title: Protective role of Galectin-3 in prion disease through regulation of microglial PrPSc uptake.
abstract: Microglia constitute a major innate defense mechanism against prion infection; however, the molecular pathways regulating microglial responses during disease progression remain incompletely understood. Galectin-3 (Gal3), a β-galactoside-binding lectin associated with reactive microglia in multiple neurodegenerative disorders, has been implicated in phagocytosis, inflammatory signaling, and lysosomal homeostasis. Here, we investigated the role of Gal3 in prion disease pathogenesis using prion-infected mice. Gal3 expression was undetectable in healthy brain but became upregulated beginning at late preclinical stages, increasing with disease progression. Gal3 localized predominantly to a subpopulation of reactive IBA1-positive microglia, particularly within the thalamus, and inversely correlated with expression of the homeostatic microglial markers P2Y12 and TMEM119, consistent with acquisition of a reactive phenotype. Microglia engaged in neuronal envelopment displayed elevated Gal3 expression during terminal disease. Constitutive deletion of Gal3 significantly accelerated clinical disease progression without altering total PrPSc accumulation, reactive gliosis, neuronal envelopment, or overall microglial and astrocytic activation. However, Gal3 deficiency markedly reduced microglial uptake of PrPSc, resulting in a lower intracellular-to-extracellular PrPSc ratio, supporting a role for Gal3 in phagocytic sequestration of prions. In contrast, Gal3 deficiency did not impair lysosomal activity, lysosomal membrane integrity, or expression of genes involved in lysosomal repair pathways. Likewise, selective inhibition of autophagy in myeloid cells exerted only minor effects on disease progression. Collectively, these findings identify Gal3 as a sensitive marker of reactive microglia that contributes to microglial uptake of PrPSc and exerts a protective role during prion disease progression.

title: TMEM106B risk converges on C-terminal fragment homeostasis: genetics, mechanisms and therapy.
abstract: TMEM106B is a genetic modifier influencing susceptibility to multiple neurodegenerative disorders, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, as well as contributing to healthy brain aging and neuronal reserve. The gene harbours single nucleotide polymorphisms and structural variants that define risk and protective haplotypes, and despite extensive efforts to identify the functional variant within these haplotypes, consensus remains elusive. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of TMEM106B genetics from human cohorts and mechanistic studies, highlighting how variants may influence its regulatory network and protein levels, with an emphasis on its aggregation-prone C-terminal domain. We further integrate evidence on the roles of TMEM106B within the endo-lysosomal system and beyond, including insights into protein structure, posttranslational modifications, interactors, proteolytic processing, and fibril formation. These findings are contextualized using data from mouse and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, highlighting current gaps in the available models and the advances required to study its functions and cleavage. Finally, we explore therapeutic strategies targeting TMEM106B, focusing on modulation of expression, specific functional pathways, and fibril formation.

title: Parkinson's at the brain border.
abstract: Parkinson's disease is increasingly recognized as a disorder that extends beyond neurons. In this issue of JEM, Stevenson et al. (https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20251245) highlight the functional consequence of α-synuclein aggregates at the brain border, uncovering their active role in reshaping lymphatic integrity and the neuroimmune macroenvironment.

title: Pathogenesis and therapeutic targets of neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease mediated by microglia lysosomal dysfunction.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein. In recent years, neuroinflammation has been recognized as a key driver in the pathogenesis of AD, and microglia, as innate immune cells of the central nervous system, play a central role in regulating the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Lysosomes are key organelles within microglia responsible for degrading pathological proteins and regulating inflammatory signaling; dysfunction of lysosomes in microglia severely impairs their ability to clear Aβ, damaged proteins, and cellular debris, thereby promoting inflammatory responses. This manuscript summarizes upstream mechanisms that may influence microglial lysosomal dysfunction from four perspectives: pathological proteins, genetic factors, lipid metabolism disorders, and proinflammatory cytokines. Pathological proteins can impair lysosomal acidification and biogenesis by interfering with key pathways such as the TFEB-v-ATPase axis; various genetic factors exacerbate functional dysregulation by influencing the expression of lysosome-related genes and lipid metabolism; lipid metabolism disorders promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, block the autophagy cascade and activate the inflammasome; proinflammatory cytokines can exert varying effects on the clearance of pathological substrates and by regulating lysosomal function. The aforementioned factors can influence microglial lysosomal function through various mechanisms, thereby contributing to impaired clearance of pathological substrates and the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Intervention strategies targeting microglial lysosomal dysfunction, including enhancing lysosomal degradation capacity, regulating autophagy related pathways, correcting cellular metabolic dysregulation and suppressing excessive neuroinflammation, may offer new avenues for AD treatment.
authors: Zi M, Ye Q, Yao M, Feng J, Meng S, Wu X, Jiang H, Yang F, Huang Y, Hu X

title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.
authors: Takahashi K, Obayashi M, Sudharsan R, Beltran WA
overview: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment.

title: Suppression of Tau-tubulin kinase 1 mitigates tau phosphorylation, and Aβ mediated neurotoxicity via altered kinase network.
abstract: Tau-tubulin kinase-1 (TTBK1) is a neuron-specific serine/threonine tau kinase that is highly expressed in the entorhinal and hippocampal regions and phosphorylates microtubule-associated protein tau at sites relevant to Alzheimer's disease (AD), thereby contributing to early tau pathology. Targeting TTBK1 can be a promising therapeutic approach for AD, although how suppression of TTBK1 may change neuronal functions is poorly understood. Here we show the proteome and phosphoproteome analysis of murine primary cortical neurons transduced with adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing short hairpin RNA (shRNA) targeting murine Ttbk1, using tandem mass tag and data independent acquisition liquid chromatography/mass-spectrometry. Suppression of TTBK1 expression by shRNA transduction increases expression of neuronal intermediate filament proteins and V1-domain subunits of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, suggesting the regulatory roles of TTBK1 on cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal activity. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces phosphorylation of TTBK1 and MAP1A as well as increases phosphorylation of neuronal intermediate filament proteins, indicating the regulation of microtubule-related proteins and axonal stabilization. Phosphosite-specific signature analysis identifies the kinases regulated by TTBK1 including AD-related cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) and AKT1. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces CDK5 activator p25/p35 ratio and pT231 phospho-tau level, consistent with the reduced activity of CDK5. Finally, silencing of Ttbk1 reduces amyloid-β-induced neurotoxicity in vitro. These results suggest a close functional relationship or coordinated regulation among TTBK1 and other kinases in maintaining axonal homeostasis via phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins, and mediating amyloid-β toxicity, thus emphasize TTBK1 as an emerging therapeutic target of AD.
authors: Yukawa K, Muraoka S, Grace S, Cafaro L, Adachi J, Ikezu T, Ikezu S

title: Translational control of microglial metabolism, inflammatory responses, and survival by the eIF4E-binding proteins.
abstract: In Alzheimer's disease (AD), activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes microglial neuroprotective functions by engaging multiple cell receptors. However, the relevant downstream effectors are not fully understood. mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) promotes mRNA translation by phosphorylating and inactivating eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1 and 2 (4E-BP1/2), which are expressed in microglia. 4E-BP1 levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are elevated in AD and correlate with markers of microglial reactivity and disease progression. Using linear regression analysis, we found that elevated CSF 4E-BP1 levels strengthen the association between soluble TREM2 levels and neurodegeneration in amyloid-positive individuals. To investigate the underlying mechanism, we performed in vitro experiments demonstrating that amyloid-β inactivated 4E-BP1 in murine microglia. The mTOR-mediated inactivation is highly dependent on Spleen Tyrosine Kinase (SYK) signaling and repeated exposure to amyloid-β impaired this process, whereas prolonged exposure increased 4E-BP1 levels in microglia. Deletion of 4E-BP1/2 resulted in increased mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation, reduced pro-inflammatory signaling, and protected microglia from amyloid-induced apoptosis. Thus, impaired 4E-BP1 inactivation-due to reduced mTOR signaling or excess 4E-BP1-disrupts immune resolution, leading to metabolic exhaustion and microglial cell death. We identify the SYK-mTORC1-4E-BP1 signaling axis as a key regulator of microglial mitochondrial biogenesis and immune resolution in AD.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
authors: Bermudez S, Choi JH, Mahmood N, Vogel JW, Almousa H, Huang Z, Kim SH, Zhu VY, Zhou L, Casas-Antillon D

title: Neuroprotective Effect of Intranasal Breast Milk-Derived Exosomes in a Neonatal Rat Model of Periventricular Leukomalacia.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) is a major cause of neurodevelopmental impairment in premature infants and is characterized by inflammation-associated white matter injury. Breast milk-derived exosomes have regenerative and immunomodulatory properties. METHODS: Experimental PVL was induced in neonatal Sprague-Dawley rats by maternal lipopolysaccharide administration. Animals were assigned to control (n=10), PVL (n=9), PVL + saline (n=10), and PVL + exosome (n=9) groups. Breast milk-derived exosomes were isolated, characterized according to MISEV2018 criteria, and administered intranasally on postnatal days 1, 3, and 5. Histopathological and biochemical analyses were performed on postnatal day 7. RESULTS: Significant differences were observed among groups in microcystic injury, myelin basic protein (MBP) staining, and tyrosine hydroxylase staining (p<0.05). Exosome treatment reduced microcystic white matter injury and preserved MBP staining intensity compared with untreated PVL groups. Tyrosine hydroxylase staining was also higher in the exosome-treated group. No significant differences were observed in GFAP staining intensity, histopathological inflammation scores, or IL-6 levels. IL-1β and TNF-α showed altered profiles, suggesting immunomodulatory effects. PKH26 labeling demonstrated exosome-associated fluorescence in the frontal cortex and hippocampus after intranasal administration. CONCLUSIONS: Intranasal breast milk-derived exosomes attenuated white matter injury and preserved markers of myelin and neuronal integrity in experimental PVL, supporting further investigation in larger models with functional outcome assessments. These findings support a potential cell-free neuroprotective strategy for inflammation-associated neonatal brain injury. However, the use of human breast milk-derived exosomes in rats and the absence of long-term functional outcomes warrant further comparative and longitudinal studies before clinical translation.

title: Protocol for imaging and analyzing the synaptic coverage of astrocytes with super-resolution STED microscopy in mouse brain slices.
abstract: Super-resolution has allowed us to image areas previously inaccessible due to the limits of standard microscopy techniques. Here, we present a protocol to determine the astroglial coverage of synapses. We detail the steps to obtain and label mouse brain slices followed by imaging using 3D stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy and analysis using a custom-made Fiji plug-in, with imaging at a lateral resolution of 80 nm. This technique ascertains the interaction between astrocytes and the glial cell's role in signaling and brain region function.
authors: Waldron L, Garnero M, Mazaud D, Rouach N
overview: Super-resolution has allowed us to image areas previously inaccessible due to the limits of standard microscopy techniques.
main: This technique ascertains the interaction between astrocytes and the glial cell's role in signaling and brain region function.

title: From Repeat Expansion to Circuit Disruption: 35 Years of Fragile X Pathophysiology.
abstract: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is caused by CGG repeat expansion in FMR1, leading to gene silencing and loss of fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP). As the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and a leading monogenic cause of autism spectrum disorder, FXS has provided an unusually tractable framework for linking a single-gene defect to abnormalities in RNA regulation, synaptic development, circuit function, and behavior. In this review, we synthesize current understanding of FMRP function, dysregulated signaling pathways, synaptic and network phenotypes, and emerging contributions from glial and human organoid models. We also evaluate therapeutic efforts, emphasizing lessons from failed targeted trials, the constraints imposed by critical developmental periods, and newer strategies aimed at restoring FMR1 itself. We argue that future progress will depend on earlier intervention, biologically informed patient stratification, and objective measures of target engagement and circuit response.
authors: Lee A, Jin P
overview: Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is caused by CGG repeat expansion in FMR1, leading to gene silencing and loss of fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein (FMRP).

title: Gαi2 promotes microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments to stabilise nascent axons in vivo.
abstract: Axon initiation is a critical step in the establishment of neuronal morphology. However, the mechanisms regulating stable axon initiation during embryonic development remain poorly understood. Here, using fixed-tissue super-resolution and high-resolution live-tissue imaging in the developing chick spinal cord, we reveal that stable axon initiation is characterised by microtubule-directed neurofilament accumulation in the emerging axon, and identify the multifunctional G-protein Gαi2 as a regulator of this process. Before axon initiation, microtubule network orientation shifts towards the site of the future axon where coiled Gαi2-associated neurofilaments accumulate asymmetrically before unfurling into the initiating axon behind microtubules. Crucially, Gαi2 is associated with neurofilaments and microtubules at their points of contact. Gαi2 depletion reduces engagement between these cytoskeletal networks and leads to impaired passage of neurofilaments into initiating axons and disrupted axon outgrowth, supporting a role for Gαi2 in regulating microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments in nascent axons. These findings advance mechanistic understanding of polarity establishment and provide insight into cytoskeletal regulation during axon formation.
authors: Higgs VE, Anwas D, Astapenka A, Toro-Tapia G, Das RM
overview: Axon initiation is a critical step in the establishment of neuronal morphology.
main: These findings advance mechanistic understanding of polarity establishment and provide insight into cytoskeletal regulation during axon formation.

title: Cucurbituril-modulated NIR emission and two-photon mitochondrial imaging of an acridine derivative.
abstract: Host-guest assemblies of an acridine dye with cucurbit[7]uril and cucurbit[8]uril give distinct NIR emissions at 674 and 708 nm, respectively. Both exhibit efficient two-photon absorption near 925 nm and successfully enable single- and two-photon mitochondrial imaging in live A549 cells.
authors: Lin X, Wu J, Shen FF, Duan LT, Wang S, Zhang ZL, Chen KH, Yu HJ, Song R

main: Both exhibit efficient two-photon absorption near 925 nm and successfully enable single- and two-photon mitochondrial imaging in live A549 cells.

title: Autism: epidemiology, genetics, molecular mechanisms, clinical features, diagnosis, and management.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Global prevalence has risen steadily, yet reported rates vary markedly across regions and populations. These discrepancies reflect inequities in diagnostic access and screening capacity rather than true differences in incidence. This review integrates recent advances across the full ASD research spectrum. We first examine global epidemiological patterns and demographic disparities. We then dissect the genetic architecture of ASD, including rare and common variants, copy number variations, and gene-environment interactions that disrupt prenatal and early postnatal brain development. At the molecular level, diverse risk factors converge on shared neurodevelopmental mechanisms. These include synaptic dysfunction, dysregulated signaling through mTOR, Ras-ERK-MAPK, Wnt and Notch pathways, impaired neurogenesis, chronic neuroimmune inflammation, and excitatory-inhibitory imbalance. We also discuss how these mechanisms manifest in core clinical features, including social deficits, repetitive behaviors, and sensory abnormalities. We summarize current diagnostic standards and their limitations. Cross-species animal models, from Drosophila to non-human primates, are evaluated for their essential roles in mechanistic validation and therapeutic screening. Finally, we assess clinical management strategies, ranging from behavioral and educational interventions to pharmacological and supportive services. By tracing a continuous path from risk factors at the population level through molecular pathophysiology to interventions guided by mechanism, this review offers an integrative synthesis that connects basic discovery to clinical translation. We further discuss how multi-omics and artificial intelligence may advance precise diagnosis rooted in mechanism and personalized treatment.
authors: Fan R, Wang Y, Miao T
overview: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors.
main: These include synaptic dysfunction, dysregulated signaling through mTOR, Ras-ERK-MAPK, Wnt and Notch pathways, impaired neurogenesis, chronic neuroimmune inflammation, and excitatory-inhibitory imbalance.

title: StrokeTime: A comprehensive longitudinal scRNA-seq atlas of the ischemic mouse brain.
abstract: Ischemic stroke triggers profound, dynamic changes in the brain's cellular landscape. To systematically characterize these dynamics, we integrated single-cell RNA-sequencing data from 21 mouse stroke studies (103 samples; 414,359 cells) spanning multiple models and post-stroke intervals. Using a harmonized computational workflow, we constructed StrokeTime, a single-cell mouse brain atlas covering hyperacute, acute, subacute, and chronic stages post-ischemia. The atlas contains 17 major cell classes and 120 fine-grained transcriptional states within myeloid, lymphoid, vascular, epithelial, neuronal, and glial populations. Myeloid cells showed the greatest plasticity, including disease-associated microglia/macrophage programs shared across resident and infiltrating cells, whereas lymphocytes featured activation and regulatory signatures within lineage constraints. Vascular and mural cells shifted from early inflammatory and barrier-disruptive programs to later fibrotic and angiogenic states. StrokeTime delineates both convergent and cell type-specific injury responses, offering a resource for studying post-ischemic brain immunity, tissue remodeling, and benchmarking future single-cell and single-nucleus studies of cerebrovascular disease.
authors: Anrather J, Garcia-Bonilla L
overview: Ischemic stroke triggers profound, dynamic changes in the brain's cellular landscape.
main: StrokeTime delineates both convergent and cell type-specific injury responses, offering a resource for studying post-ischemic brain immunity, tissue remodeling, and benchmarking future single-cell and single-nucleus studies of cerebrovascular disease.

title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

overview: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images.

title: Six3 promoting the migration and neural differentiation of BMSCs via Btg2‑mediated Akt signaling pathway activation: A therapeutic strategy for stroke.
abstract: Bone marrow‑derived mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) transplantation holds therapeutic potential for stroke; however, but its effectiveness requires optimization. The transcription factor Sine Oculis Homeobox Homolog 3 (Six3) regulates processes crucial for BMSC therapy, such as neural cell proliferation and differentiation. However, whether Six3‑modified BMSCs exert enhanced therapeutic effects on stroke remains unknown. In the present study, mouse BMSCs were isolated and identified using surface markers. Six3‑overexpressing BMSCs exhibited enhanced proliferative, migratory and neural differentiation capacities. RNA‑sequencing analysis comparing the gene expression profiles of BMSCs with and without Six3 overexpression identified BTG Anti‑Proliferation Factor 2 (Btg2) as an upregulated gene (log2FC=1.45, P<0.05) in Six3‑overexpressing cells. Further investigations revealed that Six3 directly binds to the TGATACTGTCT sequence within the Btg2 promoter and activates its transcription. Btg2 knockdown abolished the effects of Six3 overexpression. Mechanistically, Six3 promoted Akt phosphorylation via Btg2, enhancing BMSC viability and neural differentiation. A mouse model of stroke was established using transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO, 1.5‑h occlusion and 24‑h reperfusion). BMSCs were administered via tail vein injection at the onset of reperfusion. GFP expression detected in brain tissue at 24 h post‑reperfusion confirmed successful the homing of BMSCs to the brain. The transplantation of Six3‑overexpressing BMSCs ameliorated brain pathology, reducing apoptosis and cerebral infarct volume. Notably, Six3‑modified BMSCs demonstrated a significantly greater therapeutic efficacy than unmodified BMSCs. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that Six3 enhances the therapeutic properties of BMSCs by transcriptionally activating Btg2, which promotes Akt phosphorylation. These findings provide novel mechanistic insight into the optimization of stem cell therapy in stroke.
authors: Fu Z, Li Z, Zhang L, Hu W, Yang H, Wang J
overview: Bone marrow‑derived mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) transplantation holds therapeutic potential for stroke; however, but its effectiveness requires optimization.
main: The transcription factor Sine Oculis Homeobox Homolog 3 (Six3) regulates processes crucial for BMSC therapy, such as neural cell proliferation and differentiation.

title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics.
abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

overview: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions.
