title: Modeling Moyamoya disease using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells and organoids.
abstract: The underlying mechanisms of Moyamoya disease (MMD), a rare, progressive cerebrovascular disorder marked by distal internal carotid artery stenosis or occlusion and the formation of fragile collaterals, remain poorly understood, in part because conventional models fail to capture the genetic, vascular, and neurovascular complexity of human MMD. Driven by recent advances in disease modeling, MMD research has moved beyond early endothelial progenitor cell studies toward patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based platforms. Here, we summarize the generation and validation of MMD-specific iPSCs and their differentiation into endothelial cells (ECs), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), and related vascular lineages, and we discuss how two-dimensional (2D) iPSC-based models have provided insights into impaired angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, abnormal VSMC behavior, and disrupted vascular cell interactions. We then highlight the emerging use of three-dimensional vascular and neurovascular organoids, which reproduce cellular heterogeneity, vessel-like organization, and neurovascular unit interactions more closely than conventional 2D cultures. These models may provide a more integrated platform for investigating the complex vascular pathophysiology of MMD. Finally, we discuss future directions for MMD modeling, including the integration of multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-mediated genome editing with patient-derived iPSC and organoid platforms. These approaches may help clarify genotype-phenotype relationships, RNF213-dependent and RNF213-independent mechanisms, and disease-relevant molecular pathways. With further standardization and validation, iPSC- and organoid-based models could support mechanistic studies, therapeutic screening, and personalized disease modeling. Our review underscores the emerging role of patient-derived stem cell and organoid technologies in advancing MMD research and in informing future translational efforts.

title: Unraveling the Genotype-Phenotype Landscape of Kleefstra Syndrome Through EHMT1 Variant Analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Kleefstra syndrome type 1 (KLEFS1) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EHMT1, which play a key role in epigenetic regulation. Core features include global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects (CHDs), and neuropsychiatric manifestations. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with KLEFS1 evaluated at Seoul National University Hospital between January 2022 and April 2025. Genetic diagnoses were made using chromosomal microarray or whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To enhance statistical power, we conducted a joint analysis with established cohorts of at least 30 clinically characterized patients. RESULTS: Among the 15 patients with KLEFS1, 14 (93.3%) exhibited GDD or ID, with frequent comorbidities such as CHDs (8/12, 66.7%), orthopaedic manifestations (6/12, 50.0%), epilepsy (6/15, 40.0%), and sleep problems (4/11, 36.4%). Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in 10 of the 12 patients (83.3%), including pituitary anomalies in 2 (16.7%). By combining our data with recently published multicenter international cohorts, we assessed genotype-phenotype correlations by comparing the clinical features of 202 patients with different variant subtypes. Patients with multigene deletions had a significantly higher prevalence of CHDs (53.5% vs 25.8%, p value = 2 × 10-4), cortical visual impairment (12.5% vs 1.7%, p value = 0.004), microcephaly (37.1% vs 17.8%, p value = 0.009), corpus callosum abnormalities (17.9% vs 5.9%, p value = 0.02), and hearing impairment (39.7% vs 25.6%, p value = 0.04) than those with single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) or short insertions/deletions (indels), in addition to the previously identified features including epilepsy, constipation, and short stature. We also observed that a recurrent EHMT1 variant (p.Arg948Trp), identified in multiple unrelated patients, was linked to significant phenotypic heterogeneity, including late-onset neurocognitive regression. DISCUSSION: Our study showed that patients with multigene deletions are significantly more likely to exhibit multiorgan involvement, including CHDs, cortical visual impairments, microcephaly, corpus callosum abnormalities, and hearing impairments, compared with those with SNVs or indels, emphasizing the importance of genotype-informed management. We report pituitary gland abnormalities in KLEFS1, expanding the phenotypic and neuroimaging spectrum of KLEFS1. The patient showing regression in their 30s necessitates long-term, comprehensive studies to support care.

title: A PTPRO inhibitor Pi mitigates endotoxemia-induced encephalopathy-mediated blood-brain barrier disruption through cytoskeletal regulation.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Septic encephalopathy (SE) is closely associated with disruption of blood-brain barrier (BBB), resulting in neurological deficits and poor clinical outcomes. Protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) regulates disease states by dephosphorylating membrane-associated proteins and modulating intracellular signalling. Here we have examined the role of PTPRO in regulating BBB permeability and have assessed a PTPRO inhibitor (Pi) in mitigating BBB disruption during endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Genetic and pharmacological approaches, including PTPRO overexpression, knockdown or deficiency and Pi treatment, were used to evaluate endothelial dysfunction in bEND.3 cells, primary mouse brain microvascular endothelial cells and an LPS-induced murine model of endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. Barrier dysfunction, cytoskeletal remodelling and signalling events were assessed using permeability assays, immunoblotting, immunofluorescence and in vivo BBB leakage analyses. KEY RESULTS: LPS increased PTPRO expression in brain tissue from endotoxemic mice and cerebral endothelial cells. Elevated PTPRO promoted F-actin reorganization, stress fibre formation and intercellular gap formation, whereas Pi treatment or PTPRO silencing attenuated these changes. PTPRO overexpression worsened endothelial barrier dysfunction, while Pi reduced thrombin-induced permeability in bEND.3 cells and wild-type primary endothelial cells. Primary endothelial cells from PTPRO-deficient mice were protected. Mechanistically, PTPRO regulated cytoskeletal dynamics through the ErbB2-Rho-MLC2 pathway. In vivo, Pi treatment and PTPRO deficiency reduced BBB leakage, with limited effects on inflammatory cytokines. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: These findings identify PTPRO as an important regulator of BBB disruption in endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy and support pharmacological targeting of PTPRO as a potential strategy for preserving sepsis-associated BBB injury.

title: Mitochondrial apoptosis imaged by high-throughput confocal microscopy.
abstract: Mitochondrial programmed cell death (i.e. intrinsic apoptosis) is regulated through the formation of pro-apoptotic protein complexes at the mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM), which permeabilize the MOM and commit the cell to die. This step is modulated by mitochondrial dynamics. To capture this, we treated cells with the mitochondrial dynamics inhibitor M1 before inducing apoptosis with actinomycin D (ActD), and imaged them by high-throughput spinning-disk confocal microscopy. In mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) we followed apoptosis by long-term live-cell imaging, and in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) we stained fixed cells for the pro-apoptotc protein BAX at mitochondria. Here, we provide a description of these two large-scale microscopy datasets. Dataset 1 contains 637,632 images of MEFs imaged as time series after labelling of mitochondrial morphology and integrity with the mitochondrial membrane potential-sensitive dye tetramethylrhodamine-ethylester (TMRE) and apoptosis with Annexin V-FITC. The dataset also contains a digital phase contrast channel which can be useful to track cells. Dataset 2 contains 9,504 images of hiPSCs with immunofluorescence labelling of BAX and COX IV. The datasets are made available through the BioImage Archive repository.

title: Modeling human neurodegeneration with iPSCs: opportunities, limitations, and the challenge of aging.
abstract: Most neurodegenerative diseases reflect patient-specific combinations of polygenic risk variants interacting with aging and environmental factors, rather than a single causative mutation. Phase III clinical trial failure rates for neurodegenerative indications exceed 95%, reflecting in part the limitations of existing preclinical systems to fully model the human genetic context of disease. Patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have the potential to address this shortcoming by faithfully recapitulating human cell biology and preserving each patient's complete genetic architecture. This Review examines iPSC-based models of neurodegeneration across three themes. First, we discuss mechanisms revealed by these models, from convergent pathways uncovered by familial mutations to early evidence that sporadic disease biology is accessible at sufficient cohort scale. Second, we evaluate culture systems from 2-dimensional monocultures to organoids, examining how increasing complexity expands addressable biological questions while introducing trade-offs. Third, we address the aging problem: reprogramming erases epigenetic signatures of donor aging, removing the cellular context in which late-onset sporadic neurodegeneration emerges. We discuss strategies approximating aging in iPSC-derived neurons and highlight direct conversion strategies that preserve native epigenetic age, enabling access to age-dependent phenotypes. We propose a framework matching model systems to biological questions, improving mechanistic understanding and therapeutic development.

title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

title: MD2-IN-1 restores microglial lysosomal function and attenuates amyloid pathology through TREM2-associated signaling in 5×FAD mice.
abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a central regulator of microglial adaptation during Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the development of small-molecule modulators associated with TREM2 signaling remains limited. Here, through a consensus pharmacophore-guided virtual screening strategy, MD2-IN-1 was identified as a candidate small molecule associated with TREM2 signaling. Biolayer interferometry and cellular thermal shift assays supported cellular target engagement related to TREM2 (KD = 13.85 μM). In Aβ-stimulated BV2 microglia, MD2-IN-1 increased SYK phosphorylation, promoted Aβ uptake, and shifted microglial responses toward a less proinflammatory phenotype. These effects were markedly attenuated following Trem2 knockdown, indicating the involvement of the TREM2-SYK signaling pathway. Mechanistically, MD2-IN-1 restored lysosomal acidification and increased the expression of the V-ATPase subunits ATP6v0c and ATP6v0a1, accompanied by increased intracellular Aβ degradation. In 5×FAD mice, chronic MD2-IN-1 administration improved cognitive performance without detectable behavioral abnormalities compared with WT animals. Multimodal PET imaging demonstrated reduced amyloid deposition and attenuated neuroinflammatory signals, which were further supported by histological analyses showing decreased plaque burden, reduced inflammatory microglial responses, and preserved neuronal integrity. In addition, MD2-IN-1 reduced P62 accumulation and restored ATP6v0c expression in vivo, whereas these effects were partially attenuated by pharmacological inhibition of TREM2. Collectively, these findings identify MD2-IN-1 as a small-molecule modulator associated with TREM2 signaling that restores microglial lysosomal degradative function and promotes Aβ clearance in AD models, providing pharmacological support for targeting adaptive microglial responses in AD.

title: Beyond PROTACs: Conditional Technologies and New Frontiers.
abstract: This chapter surveys the post-PROTAC landscape of targeted protein degradation (TPD), covering conditional activation, new degradation modalities, and proximity-driven editing of post-translational modifications (PTMs). Condition-activated PROTACs harness prodrugs responsive to irradiation or the tumor microenvironment and nanoparticle-based platforms to achieve spatiotemporally resolved protein degradation. The targetable space is further expanded by molecular glues that recruit neosubstrates to E3 ligases, endocytosis-lysosome targeting chimeras that clear extracellular and membrane proteins, and autophagy-lysosome strategies that degrade aggregates and damaged organelles. Ribonuclease-recruiting chimeras achieve targeted RNA degradation, while the induced-proximity concept is repurposed for PTM regulation, enabling targeted glycosylation, acetylation, and phosphorylation and dephosphorylation via the recruitment of glycosyltransferases, acetyltransferases, and kinases and phosphatases. Future advances in all-small-molecule-based conditional systems, brain-targeted delivery, and regulatory frameworks informed by degradation kinetics will embed stimulus sensing and logic-gated operations into intelligent molecular systems, shifting the paradigm toward on-demand proteome and transcriptome rewiring for precision medicine.

title: Levetiracetam restores GABAergic function and network homeostasis following Vps35 deficiency in excitatory neurons.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRDs) remain incurable, partly due to their complex and poorly understood pathogenic mechanisms. Loss of vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein 35 (VPS35), a core component of the retromer complex, has been implicated in AD and ADRDs. While Vps35 deficiency is known to increase amyloidogenesis by regulating its cargo proteins, such as APP and BACE1, the precise mechanism by which VPS35 dysfunction leads to cognitive impairment remains elusive. While neuronal VPS35 regulates trafficking and functions of multiple synaptic membrane proteins, such as postsynaptic glutamatergic and GABAnergic receptors and pre-synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, and Levetiracetam (LEV), an antiepileptic drug that improves cognition, interacts with the SV2A, exactly how LEV enhances cognition is still a matter of debate. METHODS: Given the abundant expression of VPS35 in pyramidal excitatory neurons, we generated a conditional knockout mouse model with Vps35 deletion from postnatal glutamatergic excitatory neurons (Vps35CaMKIIα) and characterized its phenotypes using a combination of behavioral assessments, and electrophysiological, biochemical, and immunohiotological analyses in the hippocampal CA1 region. A targeted pharmacological screen was conducted to evaluate the therapeutic potential of LEV. RESULTS: Vps35 deletion did not disrupt the gross brain development but led to progressive cognitive decline beginning at three months of age. Electrophysiological analyses revealed earlier-onset hippocampal CA1 hyperexcitability, marked by depolarized resting membrane potentials and reduced Kir2.1 expression. However, restoring Kir2.1 to suppress hyperexcitability failed to rescue cognitive deficits. Instead, cognitive impairment was associated with weakened GABAergic transmission and disruption of the excitatory/inhibitory balance in the Schaffer collateral-CA1 circuit. Notably, LEV treatment diminished these deficits in mutant mice. Intriguingly, LEV increased the levels of retromer component, VPS26A, and multiple pre- and postsynaptic GABAergic proteins, in addition to SV2A, all of which were reduced in Vps35-deficient CA1 neurons. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify VPS35 in excitatory neurons as a critical factor for inhibitory synapse maintenance and network homeostasis. This study also highlights LEV as a potential therapeutic strategy for ADRDs through the preservation of GABAergic synapses.

title: Extracellular vesicle α-synuclein topology reveals disease-associated conformers in brain and blood.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and multiple system atrophy (MSA) are unified by pathological α-synuclein (αSyn) aggregation, yet diverge in terms of the cellular distribution of pathology and clinical phenotype. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as potential mediators or biomarkers of αSyn pathology, but whether their molecular constituents in the brain reflect disease-specific processes or conformations remains unknown. Here, we combined EV isolation, electrochemiluminescence, quantitative mass spectrometry and nanoscale single-vesicle imaging by direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy (dSTORM) to map the topology, epitope exposure and cellular origin of αSyn in EVs isolated from post-mortem PD, DLB, MSA, and healthy control (HC) brains and assessed the tractability of these molecular signatures in blood. Proteomics and immunoblotting of EV lysates isolated from human brains confirmed that they were highly purified and derived from neurons and glial cell subtypes. Across diseases, αSyn association with EVs exhibited distinct patterns: In PD and DLB, both total αSyn levels normalised to CD81 and the percentage of neuronal (L1CAM+) EVs with aggregated αSyn as detected by aggregate-preferring antibodies, were increased, whereas in MSA, aggregated αSyn was detected primarily in neuronal and to a lesser extent glial EV subpopulations without an increase in total EV-associated αSyn. Further epitope mapping by dSTORM identified a distinct αSyn conformational arrangement, as detected by antibodies against an epitope spanning αSyn residues 34-45, that was enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs in MSA compared to PD. This N-terminal immunoreactive conformer was tractable in serum and enriched on the surface of L1CAM+ EVs from MSA compared to PD patients or controls. Collectively, our findings suggest that the epitope accessibility and topology of EV-associated αSyn proteoforms, rather than their abundance alone, discriminate synucleinopathy subtypes, offering a framework for a blood-based conformational stratification of these disorders.

title: The small giant actor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases: Microtubules.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a clinically and pathologically diverse group of disorders characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment, and neuronal loss. Although research has traditionally focused on disease-associated protein misfolding and aggregation, increasing evidence implicates abnormalities of cytoskeletal organization and intracellular transport in several neurodegenerative conditions. Microtubules contribute to neuronal polarity, axonal and dendritic transport, organelle distribution, and synaptic maintenance. These functions are regulated in part by tubulin isotypes, post-translational modifications collectively described as the tubulin code, microtubule-associated proteins, and molecular motors. This narrative review examines evidence linking alterations in these processes with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and prion disease. We summarize proposed interactions among microtubule instability, impaired axonal transport, mitochondrial dysfunction, and disease-associated proteins, including tau, α-synuclein, mutant huntingtin, TDP-43, and prion protein. Evidence connecting tau pathology with microtubule dysfunction is comparatively well established in Alzheimer's disease and MAPT-related tauopathies, whereas findings in other disorders are more heterogeneous and are frequently derived from cellular or animal models. We also discuss emerging experimental approaches, candidate biomarkers, and investigational microtubule-directed treatments. However, no tubulin-specific biomarker or microtubule-targeted disease-modifying treatment discussed in this review has yet been clinically validated. Overall, microtubule dysfunction may represent one component of broader, disease-specific pathological networks rather than a universal primary cause of neurodegeneration. Further longitudinal and clinical studies are needed to determine whether microtubule-related alterations act as causes, consequences, or modifiers of disease progression.

title: Endosome-associated Rab GTPases control distinct aspects of neural circuit assembly.
abstract: Neural circuit assembly relies on the precise regulation of cell-surface receptors that mediate signaling and adhesion. Endocytosis controls receptor activity and availability by internalizing and routing proteins through early endosomes to one of two main pathways: recycling back to the cell-surface or delivery to lysosomes for degradation. Rab GTPases direct receptors into these distinct pathways, but their specific contributions to circuit formation remain opaque. Using clonal analyses with null alleles, we dissected the roles of Rab-mediated trafficking to early, late, and recycling endosomes across multiple stages of circuit assembly in vivo. Our approach revealed that Rab5 and Rab11 regulate extensive and largely distinct developmental events, highlighting the pivotal roles of early endosome sorting and recycling pathways in circuit assembly. As neurons mature, both the spatial distribution and abundance of specific endocytic compartments change to reflect evolving trafficking demands. Our findings underscore how distinct post-endocytic trafficking fates are necessary to build neural circuits.

title: CHCHD2 mitigates age-associated proteostatic collapse by maintaining homeostasis of the mitochondria-lysosome axis.
abstract: Mutations in coiled-coil-helix-coiled-coil-helix domain containing 2 (CHCHD2), including the Parkinson's disease (PD)-linked CHCHD2T61I mutation, are associated with Lewy body disorders (LBDs) by unknown mechanisms. Here, we demonstrate that CHCHD2T61I exacerbates age-related brain pathologies, including axonal degeneration and cognitive deficits, by disrupting the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Specifically, CHCHD2T61I binds and reduces cathepsin B (CTSB) and cathepsin L (CTSL) levels, inducing lysosomal membrane permeability and impairing α-synuclein fibril clearance. We also demonstrate that human CHCHD2 declines in the brain with age, while expression of wild-type CHCHD2 safeguards against age-related neuroinflammation, dopaminergic neuron loss, insoluble protein aggregation, and structural deterioration of mitochondria and lysosomes. These findings, supported by observed reductions in CTSB and CHCHD2 in human LBD brains, establish CHCHD2 as a key regulator of neuronal resilience to aging and proteostatic collapse via the mitochondria-lysosome axis. Preventing age-associated CHCHD2 decline offers a therapeutic strategy to preserve brain health throughout aging.

title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

title: KATNAL2 dysfunction impairs microtubule dynamics and contributes to syndromic neurodevelopmental disease.
abstract: Katanins are microtubule-severing ATPases. Dysfunction of katanin subunits has been implicated in impaired neurogenesis, morphogenesis, and neuronal migration. Although heterozygous variants in KATNAL2 (katanin-like 2), a known autism-spectrum disorder (ASD) risk gene, have been reported in patients with ASD or other neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), the underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a homozygous missense variant in KATNAL2 (NM_001387690.1:c.1390T>C; p.(Ser464Pro)) in a pediatric patient presenting with severe global developmental delay, intellectual disability, infantile-onset epilepsy, and autistic features, extending the phenotypic spectrum beyond prior autism-focused associations. To elucidate the cellular mechanisms underlying KATNAL2 dysfunction, we established induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patient fibroblasts and differentiated them into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) for quantitative immunofluorescence analyses of microtubule organization, microtubule regulatory proteins, and transcriptome profiling. In parallel, we generated CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants and assessed body patterning and axonal projections using the transgenic nbt:dsRed line. Patient iPSC-derived NPCs showed impaired interphase microtubule network organization with increased angular standard deviation in directionality and mitotic/cytokinetic abnormalities, including abnormal positioning of the microtubule-rich cytokinetic midbody region. In vivo, CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants showed abnormal body patterning together with disorganized motor neuron and posterior lateral line nerve axonal projections. Together, these findings support KATNAL2 as a regulator of microtubule network organization and mitotic progression in human NPCs. Our data from patient-derived NPCs and a zebrafish model provide functional evidence linking the p.(Ser464Pro) variant to an expanded syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype.

title: Beyond cell replacement: restoring organelle homeostasis as the next frontier of regenerative medicine.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) have traditionally been viewed as disorders driven by individual pathological processes, including protein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, impaired autophagy, and neuroinflammation. However, growing evidence demonstrates that these mechanisms are not isolated events but interconnected manifestations of disrupted intracellular organelle communication. Dynamic interactions among mitochondria, the ER, lysosomes, peroxisomes, and other organelles coordinate calcium signaling, bioenergetics, proteostasis, lipid metabolism, and cellular stress adaptation, thereby preserving neuronal homeostasis. Progressive disruption of this communication network represents a fundamental driver of neuronal dysfunction and degeneration, suggesting that restoration of organelle homeostasis may constitute a more effective therapeutic strategy than targeting individual molecular pathways. In parallel, regenerative medicine has evolved beyond the concept of cell replacement toward approaches that enhance the resilience and repair capacity of surviving cells. Among these, mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived secretomes and extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as promising cell-free therapeutics owing to their diverse repertoire of proteins, lipids, metabolites, cytokines, growth factors, and regulatory RNAs capable of simultaneously modulating multiple cellular pathways. Accumulating evidence indicates that these bioactive cargos modulate mitochondrial function, alleviate ER stress, improve autophagy-lysosomal activity, reduce oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, and reinforce proteostasis, collectively promoting intracellular homeostasis. Here, we propose organelle homeostasis as a promising focus for regenerative medicine and discuss how cell-free therapies may redefine therapeutic strategies for NDs by restoring the intracellular communication networks that sustain cellular resilience. Finally, we highlight current translational challenges and future opportunities for engineering next-generation cell-free therapeutics targeting complex diseases.
authors: Ferreira-Antunes F, Lima MF, Moreira A, Silva FJ, Sampaio-Marques B, Salgado AJ
overview: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) have traditionally been viewed as disorders driven by individual pathological processes, including protein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, impaired autophagy, and neuroinflammation.
main: Here, we propose organelle homeostasis as a promising focus for regenerative medicine and discuss how cell-free therapies may redefine therapeutic strategies for NDs by restoring the intracellular communication networks that sustain cellular resilience.

title: Human-Derived Motor Neuron Progenitor Cell Implantation Rescues Motor Endplates Following Peripheral Nerve Injury.
abstract: PURPOSE: Degradation of motor endplates (MEPs) following peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is a major determinant of functional recovery, as prolonged denervation renders target muscles progressively unreceptive to reinnervation. While prior studies have demonstrated that stem cell-based therapies may provide neurotrophic support following PNI, their potential effects on MEP preservation have not been well studied. We hypothesized that transplantation of human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived motor neuron progenitors (MNPs) into chronically denervated muscle would be associated with preservation of MEP architecture. METHODS: With Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee approval, chronic denervation injuries were created in mice via sciatic nerve transection. After 4 months of denervation, when MEPs have consistently degraded in this animal model, the denervated tibialis anterior (TA) was injected with low-dose MNPs (10,000 cells), high-dose MNPs (500,000 cells), or phosphate-buffered saline (negative control). Using a previously established method, hiPSCs were differentiated into functional MNPs prior to injection. At selected time points post-injection, the TA was harvested and immunostained to confirm MNP viability and detect the presence of MEPs. RESULTS: Transplanted MNPs remained viable within host muscle at both evaluated time points. No identifiable MEPs were detected in phosphate-buffered saline-treated chronically denervated muscle. In contrast, MNP-treated muscles demonstrated the presence of MEP-like structures following prolonged denervation. Qualitative differences in MEP density and morphologic complexity were observed between treatment groups, with greater preservation seen in the higher-dose cohort. Contralateral uninjured muscles demonstrated intact native MEP architecture. CONCLUSIONS: Intramuscular transplantation of hiPSC-derived MNPs into chronically denervated muscle was associated with preservation of MEP morphology in this preclinical proof-of-concept model. These preliminary findings suggest that cellular therapies may represent a potential adjunctive strategy to preserve end-organ receptivity following delayed peripheral nerve injury. TYPE OF STUDY/LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Preclinical controlled animal study, Level V.

title: TPPU, a soluble epoxide hydrolase inhibitor, mitigates Aβ-induced neurotoxicity via dual modulation of mitochondrial stabilization and JNK suppression.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, primarily driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) aggregation and neuronal apoptosis. This study aims to investigate the neuroprotective effects of soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH) inhibition against Aβ-induced cytotoxicity in PC-12 cells, focusing on cell viability, apoptosis, and the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling pathway. Western blotting and fluorometric assays revealed elevated sEH expression and activity in Aβ1-42-treated PC-12 cells compared to untreated controls. Treatment with N-[1-(1-Oxopropyl)-4-piperidinyl]-N'-[4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenyl]urea (TPPU), a potent sEH inhibitor, significantly attenuated Aβ-induced apoptosis in PC-12 cells and enhanced cell viability. These findings were corroborated by CCK-8 assays and flow cytometry analyses. Furthermore, TPPU reversed Aβ-induced cleaved Caspase-3 dysregulation and restored mitochondrial membrane potential. Notably, exogenous administration of epoxyeicosatrienoic acids partially mimicked the protective effects of TPPU, primarily by preserving mitochondrial function. Western blot analysis confirmed that TPPU pretreatment suppressed the phosphorylation of JNK, thereby contributing to its anti-apoptotic effects. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that TPPU attenuates Aβ-induced neurotoxicity via dual mechanisms-restoring mitochondrial function and suppressing JNK activation-highlighting its potential as a therapeutic agent for AD.

title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. METHODS: We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. RESULTS: SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. INTERPRETATION: We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. title: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
abstract: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.

title: Time-lapse RESOLFT nanoscopy empowered by deep learning.
abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

title: Antisense Oligonucleotides that Are Toxic to Prion-Infected Mice Share an Emergent Mechanism.
abstract: Some, but not all, gapmer antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) delivered into cerebrospinal fluid exhibit fatal subacute toxicity in late-stage prion-infected mice but not in uninfected mice. Here, we performed a battery of in vivo studies demonstrating that the toxicity is compound- and disease- stage-dependent, and not predicted by behavioral or molecular measurements in uninfected animals. A panel of toxic ASOs all elicited a consistent transcriptomic response signature in prion-infected mice, which emerged over the course of 7 days post dose. This signature, driven chiefly by decreased expression of a specific set of astrocyte-expressed genes, was absent in uninfected mice receiving the same ASOs, was absent, less intense, and/or more transient in infected mice receiving tolerated ASOs, and was distinct from the transcriptomic effect of prion disease itself. Our data argue that the toxicity is an interaction between ASO and prion disease at high doses for specific compounds, and does not represent an exacerbation of ASO toxicity nor of prion disease.

title: Multiple motor proteins regulate TDP-43 anterograde axonal transport.
abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is an RNA-binding protein essential for RNA metabolism. Under physiological conditions, it predominantly resides in the nucleus but is also expressed in the cytoplasm, where it regulates mRNA trafficking and local translation. In nearly 97% of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases, TDP-43 undergoes nuclear depletion and cytoplasmic aggregation. While its nuclear functions are well characterized, its axonal roles remain poorly understood, despite axonal degeneration being a hallmark of ALS pathology. To address this gap, we investigated TDP-43 localization and transport dynamics in axons of H9-derived human neurons. We compared fluorescently labeled TDP-43 with three well-characterized axonal cargoes, ras-related protein Rab5, synaptophysin, and amyloid precursor protein, and examined protein-protein interactions between TDP-43 and the axonal transport machinery. Our analyses revealed that TDP-43 exhibits active anterograde axonal transport and interacts with multiple kinesin motor proteins, including all three KIF5 isoforms, through the adaptor KLC1, and the synaptic vesicles motor KIF1A. This multi-motor engagement suggests a flexible transport system that ensures mRNA delivery to distal axons. In ALS, where TDP-43 accumulates abnormally in the cytoplasm, this flexibility may become compromised, with multiple transport mechanisms simultaneously affected. This could contribute to progressive accumulation of non-functional TDP-43 granules, disrupting mRNA trafficking and local translation. Our findings provide a foundation for understanding how physiological TDP-43 transport mechanisms may be impaired during disease, highlighting axonal TDP-43 transport pathways as potential therapeutic targets.

title: The postsynaptic scaffold protein ABLIM1 regulates seizure susceptibility by maintaining GluA2 membrane localization in chronic epilepsy.
abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common form of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in adults, is a frequent chronic neurological disorder. Nevertheless, the precise pathophysiological mechanisms underlying TLE remain largely undefined. Our findings demonstrate that Actin-binding LIM protein 1 (ABLIM1) is broadly expressed in the adult mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus. The protein is primarily localized to neurons, enriched in the postsynaptic density (PSD), colocalizes with the scaffold protein PSD95, and directly binds to F-actin. Co-IP experiments confirmed that ABLIM1 interacts with the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) subunits GluA1 and GluA2. Following hippocampal stereotaxic injection of adeno-associated virus (AAV) to specifically knock down ABLIM1 expression, we observed reduced F-actin polymerization, decreased dendritic spine density, and thinning of the PSD in the mouse hippocampus. In the chronic epilepsy models induced by kainic acid (KA), ABLIM1 knockdown significantly exacerbated seizure severity and increased seizure susceptibility. Further mechanistic studies revealed that ABLIM1 knockdown specifically reduces membrane expression of GluA2 without altering its total protein levels. Collectively, ABLIM1 may regulate epileptogenesis and disease progression by maintaining postsynaptic structural integrity and GluA2 membrane homeostasis. Thus, the ABLIM1-GluA2 signaling axis represents a potential therapeutic target for DRE.

title: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson's mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms.
abstract: Synaptojanin 1 is a brain enriched phosphoinositide phosphatase implicated in endocytosis at the synapse. A mutation (R258Q) that selectively impairs its Sac1 phosphatase domain causes early onset familial Parkinsonism. Neurons of mice with this mutation display synaptic vesicle traffic defects across the brain, but selective dystrophic changes in a subset of dopaminergic axons in the dorsolateral striatum. Using correlative light microscopy-FIB-SEM of mutant mouse striata to visualize in 3D these abnormal structures we show that they represent clusters of focal axonal dilations harboring massive, onion-like DAT enriched plasma membrane infoldings, generally localized next to cell bodies of neighboring cells, often engulfing evaginations of such cells. This dysmorphia was associated with a deficit in dopamine release in the same striatal region. Given the involvement of Synj1 in endocytic mechanisms, these structures may reflect an imbalance between exocytosis and endocytosis. Their occurrence only in a subset of axons suggests a vulnerability threshold of these axons beyond which the expansion of the plasma membrane is not counteracted by compensatory mechanisms.

title: Macroscopic cerebral energy efficiency corresponds to neuron reorganization in awake and anesthetized mice.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Non-invasive imaging of brain function and energy supply is crucial for diagnosing and treating brain disorders. Conventional imaging struggles to capture altered relationships between energy supply and demand caused by brain diseases. A novel method, thus far only tested non-invasively in human subjects, is to calculate relative power (rPWR) and relative cost (rCST) to assess cerebral energy efficiency. However, whether rPWR/rCST tracks individual changes and relate to neural activity remains unproven. METHODS: Our study examines awake and anesthetized male mice and compares rPWR/rCST with invasive two-photon microscopy. RESULTS: We found that rPWR/rCST distributions were similar between awake mice and humans, but changed in anesthetized mice, indicating a shift in the brain's economic balance. Furthermore, changes in rPWR/rCST were linked to the reorganization of microscopic neural networks, observed with two-photon microscopy. DISCUSSION: Our work highlights the potential of rPWR/rCST for medical applications, and that neural network reorganization is linked to the brain's economic balance.

title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

title: Distinct Regulatory Logic Controls Recruitment and Membrane Dynamics of ESCRT-III Subunit Vps60.
abstract: Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery drives membrane remodeling and scission events essential for multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis. The accessory ESCRT-III subunit Vps60 (mammalian CHMP5) shares structural features with the major polymerizing subunit Snf7, including the capacity to form homopolymers in vitro. Here, we demonstrate in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that Vps60 recruitment and polymerization require conditions that permit Snf7 polymer turnover: Vps60 is largely excluded when Snf7 assembly is absent and when Snf7 disassembly is blocked, consistent with recruitment of Vps60 late in the ESCRT-III cycle to Snf7 assemblies that undergo normal turnover. Structure-function analysis reveals that Vps60 regulation diverges fundamentally from core ESCRT-III subunits: while occlusion of the Vps60 C terminus by a GFP tag drives constitutive membrane association and polymer assembly, C-terminal truncation impairs endosomal recruitment, indicating that the Vps60 C terminus is required for membrane recruitment, in contrast to the autoinhibitory C-terminal domains of core ESCRT-III subunits. A C-terminally tagged Vps60 that constitutively associates with membranes phenocopies loss of Vps60 function in both intralumenal vesicle (ILV) formation and cargo sorting. These findings indicate that despite structural similarity to Snf7, Vps60 functions as a late-arriving accessory factor whose recruitment and assembly are tightly coupled to Snf7 dynamics. title: TRPML3 and TRPML1/3 differentially regulate unconventional MIF secretion through TMED10 and secretory autophagy.
abstract: The intracellular Ca2+ channel TRPML3 regulates autophagy by multimerization in a phosphoinositide (PIP)-dependent manner; however, its role in other membrane dynamics remains unclear. Here, we report that TRPML3 regulates type III unconventional protein secretion (UcPS) through two distinct pathways: TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy. TRPML3 interacted with TMED10 and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a signal sequence-lacking pleiotropic cytokine whose secretion mechanism has remained undefined. We found that cytosolic MIF is transported to membrane-enclosed compartments through TMED10-channeled UcPS. Notably, TRPML3, but not TRPML1 or TRPML1/3, promoted TMED10 oligomerization, thereby enhancing MIF secretion in a Ca2+-independent manner. Furthermore, once translocated into vesicular compartments, MIF colocalized with LC3, and its secretion was dependent on secretory autophagy. Mechanistically, we identified PI(3,4)P2 as a key regulator of secretory autophagy, with TRPML1/3 acting downstream of PI(3,4)P2 to mediate Ca2+-dependent MIF secretion. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that MIF is a novel cargo of type III UcPS, operating through TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy, which are regulated by TRPML3 in a Ca2+-independent manner and by the PI(3,4)P2-TRPML1/3 axis in a Ca2+-dependent manner, respectively.

title: Mechanism of fluoride-induced neurotoxicity: Dissecting a multi-target organelle signaling network.
abstract: Fluoride is a widely distributed environmental contaminant, and excessive exposure has been associated with adverse neurological outcomes. However, the underlying mechanisms of fluoride-induced neurotoxicity remain incompletely understood. In this review, we integrate current evidence to propose a multilevel, multi-target mechanistic framework of fluoride-induced neurotoxicity. We highlight that fluoride exerts neurotoxic effects not via isolated pathways but through the coordinated disruption of multiple organelles, particularly mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and lysosomes. Dysfunction of these organelles converges via inter-organelle crosstalk, leading to impaired energy metabolism, calcium dyshomeostasis, defective protein folding, and impaired lysosomal degradation. We further identify oxidative stress as a central integrative relay and amplifier, linking organelle dysfunction to downstream pathological processes, including neuroinflammation, neuronal cell death, and synaptic impairment. Emerging evidence also suggests that epigenetic reprogramming, including aberrant DNA methylation and non-coding RNA network remodeling, contributes to long-term gene expression changes. These molecular and cellular disturbances ultimately converge on impaired neurogenesis, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive deficits. Finally, we discuss current limitations, including the dependence on high-dose experimental models, and propose future directions emphasizing multi-target strategies to restore organelle homeostasis and redox balance. This integrative framework provides a comprehensive perspective on fluoride-induced neurotoxicity and may facilitate the development of more effective intervention strategies.
authors: Li Q, Du Y, Zeng Y, Cheng Y, Du R, Yan X, Yu F, Ba Y, Zhou G
overview: Fluoride is a widely distributed environmental contaminant, and excessive exposure has been associated with adverse neurological outcomes.
main: These molecular and cellular disturbances ultimately converge on impaired neurogenesis, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive deficits.

title: Convergent molecular mechanisms of chronic heavy metal exposure and repetitive mild traumatic brain injury in neurodegenerative processes.
abstract: Repetitive mild traumatic brain injury (rmTBI) and chronic environmental exposure to heavy metals represent widespread contributors to neurological dysfunction that are typically studied independently. However, emerging evidence indicates that these insults converge on overlapping cellular pathways that disrupt neuronal homeostasis, redox balance, genomic stability and proteostasis, including tau regulation. Notably, environmental metals including mercury, lead, arsenic, cadmium, and hexavalent chromium induce oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammatory signaling, processes that are also central to rmTBI pathophysiology. In this review, we synthesize mechanistic and clinical evidence linking chronic heavy metal exposure and rmTBI and examine how their interaction may influence long-term vulnerability to neurodegeneration. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate these two domains within a unified mechanistic framework. We first summarize shared and metal-specific mechanisms of heavy metal neurotoxicity and integrate these findings with the cellular and systemic consequences of rmTBI. Attention is given to higher-order convergent processes, including disruption of the blood-brain barrier, dysregulation of the gut-brain axis, protein misfolding and tau pathology, ferroptosis, and impairment of proteostatic and autophagic pathways. We also discuss emerging biomarker signatures and therapeutic targets relevant to combined environmental and traumatic exposures. Collectively, current evidence supports a model in which chronic heavy metal burden may diminish neural resilience and could increase vulnerability to the cumulative effects of rmTBI. Although direct evidence of their interaction remains limited, the substantial mechanistic overlap provides a framework for future studies investigating environmental contributions to post-traumatic neurodegeneration, biomarker discovery, and potential therapeutic strategies.

main: We also discuss emerging biomarker signatures and therapeutic targets relevant to combined environmental and traumatic exposures.

title: Autolysosomal enhancer GHF201 attenuates pathophysiology in a mucopolysaccharidosis type I mouse model.
abstract: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS-I) is a hereditary lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency in the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase (IDUA) leading to pathogenic over-accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major constituent of connective tissue and mediators of cell signaling. We tested the therapeutic efficacy of the autolysosomal activator GHF201 in the Idua -/- mouse model of MPS-I. We show that GHF201 reduced GAGs and increased cathepsin activity in Idua -/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and brain cells. In vivo GHF201 improved aberrant locomotion and behavior, reduced interstitial cathepsins in joints and liver, increased systemic catabolism, corrected bone dysplasia, increased autophagic flux, and ameliorated CNS neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation. GHF201 also reduced brain N-glycans, which are degraded in lysosomes. In conclusion, the lysosomal and autophagic activator GHF201 was demonstrated to improve various pathophysiological parameters in MPS-I-modeling Idua -/- female mice. Our results suggest that GHF201 can complement the inadequate Aldurazyme enzyme replacement therapy as an add-on therapy.

title: Astrocytes regulate axonal mitochondrial transport deficits in C9ORF72 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis motor neurons.
abstract: Disrupted axonal transport and astrocyte dysfunction are implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Here we show these processes are linked-human-induced pluripotent stem-cell-derived astrocytes carrying the C9ORF72 mutation disrupt mitochondrial axonal transport and mitochondrial function in cocultured motor neurons (MNs). Conversely, isogenic gene-corrected astrocytes or boosting astrocytic mitochondrial bioenergetics rescue axonal mitochondrial transport deficits in C9ORF72 MNs. Our results delineate a non-cell-autonomous role for astrocytes in regulating mitochondrial transport along axons in ALS models.

title: VPS13A loss of function mutations cause disruption of cellular calcium homeostasis and increase the vulnerability to ferroptosis.
abstract: VPS13A belongs to the family of bridge-like lipid transfer proteins, which connect opposing membranes at organelle contact sites in order to facilitate bulk lipid transfer. Loss of function mutations in the VPS13A gene cause VPS13A disease. Diminished store operated calcium entry has previously been described in patient-derived fibroblasts and iPSC-derived neurons from VPS13A disease patients and impairments in mitochondrial calcium uptake was observed in patient-derived fibroblasts. However, how calcium (dys)homeostasis is regulated and its effects on neuronal survival remain enigmatic. Here, we investigated calcium regulation and cell death in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons from VPS13A disease patients. We demonstrate that reduced store operated calcium entry is associated with diminished plasma membrane-ER contact sites and altered expression of the calcium release-activated calcium channel ORAI1. VPS13A-deficient neurons further exhibited elevated mitochondrial calcium levels, as well as resistance of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter to inhibition by Ru360. Further, VPS13A disease neurons show increased lipid peroxidation, driving ferroptotic cell death. These findings establish a mechanistic link between disrupted calcium homeostasis and neuronal degeneration in VPS13A disease and identify calcium (dys)homeostasis and ferroptosis as potential pathogenic pathways and therapeutic targets.

overview: VPS13A belongs to the family of bridge-like lipid transfer proteins, which connect opposing membranes at organelle contact sites in order to facilitate bulk lipid transfer.
main: We demonstrate that reduced store operated calcium entry is associated with diminished plasma membrane-ER contact sites and altered expression of the calcium release-activated calcium channel ORAI1.

title: Paeonol alleviates oxidative stress and brain injury in hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy by activating the PI3K/Akt/Nrf2 signaling pathway.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) is a severe neonatal neurological disorder, in which oxidative stress serves as a central mediator of brain injury. Paeonol (Pae), a phenolic compound with established anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, remains underexplored as a therapeutic strategy for HIE. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of Pae against HIE-induced brain injury and explored whether its protective effects involves attenuation of oxidative stress through activation of the PI3K/Akt/Nrf2 signaling pathway. METHODS: A neonatal rat HIE model was established using the modified Rice-Vannucci method. Brain injury, oxidative stress markers, and neurological function were assessed through histological staining and behavioral testing. Network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations were used to identify and validate potential targets. An H2O2-induced oxidative stress model in PC12 cells was employed for mechanistic validation, with PI3K and Nrf2 pharmacologically inhibited using LY294002 and ML385, respectively. RESULTS: Pae significantly reduced cerebral infarct volume and histopathological alterations, attenuated oxidative stress, and improved motor and cognitive performance in HIE rats. Network pharmacology identified the PI3K/Akt as a key target pathway, while molecular docking revealed a strong binding affinity between Pae and AKT1. Consistently, Pae activated the PI3K/Akt pathway, promoted Nrf2 nuclear translocation, and upregulated HO-1 expression in both in vivo and in vitro experiments; these effects were substantially reversed by LY294002 and ML385. CONCLUSION: Pae ameliorates HIE-induced brain injury and neurological deficits via activation of the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway and reinforcement of Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defenses. These findings identify Pae as a preclinical neuroprotective candidate worthy of further exploration.
authors: Hu D, Li J, Ye L, Yan J, Lei S, Zhang G, Lin L, Lin Q
overview: BACKGROUND: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) is a severe neonatal neurological disorder, in which oxidative stress serves as a central mediator of brain injury.
main: RESULTS: Pae significantly reduced cerebral infarct volume and histopathological alterations, attenuated oxidative stress, and improved motor and cognitive performance in HIE rats.

title: Celastrol attenuates testosterone-induced benign prostatic hyperplasia by modulating the PTEN/PI3K/AKT pathway.
abstract: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) represents a prevalent urological disease observed primarily among aging men. Celastrol (CELA) is an active natural compound with diverse pharmacological properties. The primary aim of this research is to assess the potential protective activity of CELA in testosterone (TEST)-induced BPH in rats. Male Wistar rats were allocated into six distinct groups for treatment: group 1 acted as the control and was given the vehicle; group 2 received only CELA (2 mg/kg, orally); group 3 was administered TEST alone (3 mg/kg, subcutaneously); groups 4 and 5 were administered the combination of TEST (3 mg/kg, subcutaneously) and CELA (1 or 2 mg/kg, orally); and group 6 received a combination of TEST (3 mg/kg, subcutaneously) and finasteride (FINA) (0.5 mg/kg, orally). Over a period of four weeks, CELA at doses of 1 or 2 mg/kg effectively inhibited the increase in both the prostate index and weight when compared to rats treated with TEST. CELA mitigated pathological alterations in prostate architecture, reduced the proliferation markers and modulated the expression of apoptosis markers compared to TEST-treated rats. Furthermore, CELA exhibited antioxidant properties by mitigating the TEST-induced increase in lipid peroxide levels and the depletion of superoxide dismutase and catalase activities. Moreover, CELA exhibited anti-inflammatory activity by significantly downregulating tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6, and nuclear factor-κB expression. In addition, CELA elevated phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) and reduced phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and AKT expression compared with the TEST group. In addition, CELA inhibited TEST-induced enhancement of mRNA expression of 5α-reductase type 2, androgen receptor and fibroblast growth factor 2. Overall, CELA partially alleviates TEST-induced BPH in rats, an effect that is associated with modulation of PTEN/PI3K/AKT axis.

title: Volume electron microscopy reveals oligodendrocyte axon selection patterns and spatial assembly of myelin and nodes.
abstract: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple axons, requiring single cells to coordinate target selection, sheath growth, and node formation across complex cortical geometry. We combined serial block-face electron microscopy, complete segmentation, and three-dimensional reconstruction to analyze early-myelinating oligodendrocytes in the somatosensory cortex of a postnatal day 14 rat at single-cell and nanoscale resolution. Individual oligodendrocytes initiated myelination across all contacted axons, while early ensheathment decreased with increasing process distance from the soma. Each oligodendrocyte also contacted axons within a restricted caliber range, independently of wrapping progression. At prospective nodes of Ranvier, transient cytoplasmic projections extended into axonal domains from adjacent oligodendrocytes and converged near presumptive paranodes. These observations support a structural model in which oligodendrocyte geometry, cell-specific axon selection, and intercellular interactions jointly organize early cortical myelination and nodal assembly, providing testable hypotheses for developmental myelination and repair after demyelination.

title: Rod photoreceptors have a dual dependency on both aerobic glycolysis and OXPHOS and diverge metabolically from other retinal neurons.
abstract: The retina metabolizes glucose into lactate, a hallmark of aerobic glycolysis known as the Warburg effect. Although evidence points to rod photoreceptors as the primary source of aerobic glycolysis, a comparison of the energy metabolism in different retinal neurons has yet to be performed. We combined two-photon fluorescence lifetime imaging of biosensors with pharmacological protocols to analyze metabolic dynamics in healthy and diseased rod photoreceptors and RBPMS-positive ganglion and calretinin-positive amacrine cells. Our data reveal distinct metabolic profiles among retinal neurons, identify rods as the drivers of aerobic glycolysis, demonstrate that inner retinal neurons rely on oxidative phosphorylation, show that rods need both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation to maintain ATP levels, and suggest that rods can metabolize lactate. A mutation causing retinitis pigmentosa increases lactate production in rods but changes the energy metabolism only subtly otherwise. Our results improve the understanding of retinal physiology and are relevant for pathologies involving imbalanced energy metabolism.

title: MIMAS: An open-source microlens-array miniature microscope for accessible large-field cortical imaging in freely behaving mice.
abstract: Large-scale cortical dynamics during natural behavior are difficult to measure because head-mounted imaging systems must balance field of view, spatial resolution, weight, and optical complexity. Existing wide-field miniature microscopes often rely on compound or custom-corrected optical assemblies, which increase device complexity and limit accessibility for laboratories without specialized optics expertise. Here, we present the Miniature Integrated Microlens Array System (MIMAS), an open-source head-mounted fluorescence microscope that replaces conventional multi-element optics with a 4 × 5 microlens array as its sole imaging element. By combining modular subfield acquisition with computational registration and stitching, MIMAS achieves cellular-resolution imaging across an approximately 4 × 4.5 mm2 field of view while weighing only 2.31 g. In freely behaving mice with sparse labeling of layer 2/3 cortical neurons, MIMAS enabled simultaneous calcium imaging across multiple dorsal cortical regions, with signals extracted from thousands of neurons. This broad sampling captured distributed cortical activity related to locomotor state and sparse position-modulated responses during open-field exploration without detectable disruption of locomotion or loss of signal quality over 30 min of recording. Beyond neuronal imaging, MIMAS also supported wide-field vascular imaging and resolved vessel caliber-dependent hemodynamic responses to isoflurane. These results establish MIMAS as a lightweight, accessible, and versatile platform for large-scale fluorescence imaging in freely behaving mice and demonstrate an alternative strategy for wide-field cortical imaging that lowers the optical complexity barrier for individual laboratories.

title: Dorsal horn mapping: a Fiji toolbox for standardized laminar registration and transparent reporting of spinal cord imaging data from adult C57Bl/6 mice.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Rexed's laminae provide the anatomical framework for interpreting the spatial organization of neuronal populations within the spinal dorsal horn and are therefore widely used to describe immunohistochemical, in situ hybridization, and functional imaging data. However, despite their widespread use, no standardized approach for assigning cells to individual laminae has been established, limiting reproducibility and direct comparison of datasets across studies. METHODS: We developed Dorsal Horn Mapping, an open-source Fiji toolbox that implements a standardized workflow for laminar registration in transverse mouse spinal cord sections. The toolbox aligns segment-specific reference maps to experimental images using user-guided rigid transformations and independent scaling, assigns labeled cells to Rexed's laminae, and transforms their positions into a common spatial reference frame. In addition, it provides tools for quantitative laminar analysis and visualization of pooled datasets as composite reference maps. RESULTS: Validation experiments demonstrated high inter-user reproducibility of template alignment and laminar assignment across users with different levels of anatomical expertise. Registrations showed good agreement with established laminar markers and resulted in highly consistent assignment of neuronal populations to individual laminae. Thus, 81% of IB4-pos pixels were mapped to lamina II (95% CI: 68.4-86.2%) and the estimated difference in cell counts averaged across all users, segments and laminae was 0.08 cells (95% CI: -0.68 to 0.83; P = 0.843). Analysis of representative multichannel immunohistochemical datasets further demonstrated the utility of the workflow for standardized visualization and quantitative analysis of cellular localization. CONCLUSION: Dorsal Horn Mapping provides an accessible framework for standardized laminar registration and transparent spatial reporting of spinal cord imaging data from adult C57BL/6 mice. By introducing a common spatial reference system for dorsal horn anatomy, the toolbox facilitates direct comparison of cellular localization across experiments and laboratories and has the potential to improve reproducibility, comparability, and reporting standards in pain and spinal cord research.

title: EasyQuant: A machine-learning-assisted imaging-based tool for quantifying neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).
abstract: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) play a crucial role in host defense, yet their dysregulation is associated with inflammation and tissue damage. Consequently, researching NETs in vitro is essential for understanding their role in both health and disease. However, accurate quantification of NETs in vitro remains a challenge due to limitations in manual methods and semi-automated tools, which often require extensive user input and/or are time-consuming. Moreover, some methods identify neutrophils and NETs based on a single fixed parameter, such as size, which may lead to inaccuracies in recognizing neutrophils due to the cells' biological complexity. In this study, we developed a user-friendly framework for NET quantification using LABKIT, an ImageJ plugin, together with a custom Jython-based script that streamlines image processing and NET classification. By combining fluorescence microscopy with a machine learning tool, this approach enables rapid, scalable analysis of large multi-dimensional datasets with improved flexibility, reliability, and accessibility. Leveraging LABKIT for quantification ensures objective and consistent segmentation of NETs and neutrophils, reducing user bias and processing time while supporting reproducible data curation. Overall, EasyQuant provides a foundation for a freely accessible pipeline that can be integrated into diverse research workflows, herein specifically applied to improve the accuracy and throughput of neutrophil quantification.

title: BVLab-analyzer: a unified visual toolbox for terabyte-scale whole-brain cell detection, neuron reconstruction, and vascular network extraction.
abstract: BVLab-Analyzer is a standalone graphical software tool for end-to-end analysis of terabyte-scale whole-brain microscopy images. Operating through a zero-code interface, it handles data import (TIFF, BioImageVision, OME-Zarr), deep learning-based semantic segmentation, 3D skeleton reconstruction, and morphological statistical analysis within a unified pipeline. The software supports three target structures-cells, neurons and vasculature-and exports their morphological reconstructions in standard SWC format. To accelerate training data preparation, Smart Annotation tools provide sub-volume interference isolation, coarse-vessel ray tracing, and skeleton auto-interpolation. For inference, optimized block-wise strategies enable a standard 3D U-Net to predict whole-brain volumes up to 12 TB on a single consumer-grade GPU, while an interrupt-and-resume engine ensures fault tolerance during extended computations. By integrating these features, BVLab-Analyzer lowers the hardware barrier for whole-brain analysis and unifies previously fragmented toolchains-from annotation and segmentation to reconstruction and quantification-into a single, accessible software environment.

title: Therapeutic potential of neural stem cell-derived exosomes and PRP in Parkinson's disease: A novel regenerative approach.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurological ailment characterized by oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. The current treatments lack disease-modifying capabilities. The current study investigated the neuroprotective and regenerative efficacy of a combination of neural stem cell-derived exosomes (NMSC-EXO) and PRP in a rotenone-induced rat model of PD. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Thirty male Wistar rats were randomly assigned to three equal groups (n = 10/group). Group I (negative Control): received subcutaneous (s.c) sunflower oil for 35 days followed by intravenous (i.v.) saline for 30 days. Group II (Rotenone model): administered 2 mg/kg/day rotenone s.c. for 35 days followed by i.v. saline for 30 days; Group III Rotenone + combination (Exosomes + PRP): received 2 mg/kg/day rotenone s.c. for 35 days, followed by biweekly i.v. injection of 109 NMSC-EXO in 250 μl PRP for 30 days. Evaluation starts 65 days from the beginning, evaluation included behavioural assessments (wire hanging, ladder climbing, open field), histological and immunohistochemical evaluation of substantia nigra (tyrosine hydroxylase [TH] and caspase 1), qRT-PCR gene expression (integrin [Itg] and [TH]), as well as oxidative stress markers (GSH and MDA). RESULTS: The co-administration of NMSC-EXO and PRP significantly attenuated rotenone-induced motor deficits, thereby restoring locomotor activity, balance, and exploratory behavior. Dual therapy preserved dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, downregulated the apoptotic marker caspase-1, and significantly decreased lipid peroxidation (MDA) while restoring reduced glutathione (GSH) levels. Furthermore, treatment led to significant upregulation of tyrosine hydroxylase and integrin expression relative to the rotenone model group. CONCLUSION: Combined NMSC-EXO and PRP therapy exerted strong neuroprotective, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic effects against rotenone-induced neurotoxicity. This synergetic approach represents a novel, cell-free regenerative strategy for Parkinson's disease.
authors: Farid MF, F Tohamy A, Ibrahim MA, Ma M, Rizk H
overview: INTRODUCTION: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurological ailment characterized by oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.

title: Primary cilium as a sensory organelle and metabolic hub in health and diseases.
abstract: Primary cilia are microtubule-based organelles protruding from the cell surface, which are conventionally understood as passive cellular antennae that detect extracellular stimuli. However, emerging evidence redefines these microtubule-based organelles as dynamic, bidirectional hubs that integrate environmental sensing with cellular metabolic adaptation. By selectively compartmentalizing receptors, ion channels, transporters, and signaling components, they function as specialized signal-processing compartments that receive, integrate, amplify, and relay information to coordinate cellular metabolism, adaptation, and cell-fate determination. Cilia-dependent signaling pathways regulate glucose and lipid metabolism, Ca2⁺ and second-messenger dynamics, and mitochondrial homeostasis. Conversely, environmental and metabolic changes remodel ciliary structure, molecular composition, and signaling competence. In this review, we present primary cilia as a bidirectional interface between environmental sensing and metabolic adaptation. We discuss how cilia respond to nutrient availability, mechanical forces, and oxygen tension, and how disruption of this sensory-metabolic interface contributes to metabolic, cardiovascular, reproductive, neurodegenerative, and cancer-related diseases. Defining the cellular and environmental contexts in which ciliary remodeling is protective or pathogenic will be essential for translating cilia biology into therapeutic strategies.
